JUSTICE ALEX FINLAYSON

PART I:         OVERVIEW

[
1
]

The parties cohabited for 7 years and 5 months, from November 1, 2012
until their agreed upon date of separation of April 3, 2020.    There was a
period between about August of 2017 and March of 2018 that the parties
maintained separate residences, while still in a relationship.  Despite their
agreement as to an April 3, 2020 date of separation, they nevertheless continued
in some form of a relationship with one another, either until the end of 2020
as the father maintained, or until as late as July of 2023 as the mother
maintained.

[
2
]

The child at the center of this case is L.  She turned 13 while this
Judgment was under reserve.

[
3
]

L. has been stuck in the middle of interminable, extreme conflict,
between her parents.  That conflict continued to manifest itself throughout
this trial, right up until its end.   The parents’ relationship with one
another was toxic.  L.’s relationship with her father is now fractured.

[
4
]

Clearly the most significant issue for this trial was what parenting
arrangements should be put in place for L.  The parents litigated numerous incidents
of conflict that had occurred between them over the years.  They each sought to
demonstrate the consequential impact of that conflict on themselves and their
daughter, while also seeking findings about who is to blame.  But parenting was
not all that was in issue during this trial.

[
5
]

There were two core financial issues also, being the division of their jointly
owned residence in Thornhill (the “Thornhill Property”) and child support.  There
were numerous other related financial issues about the validity of two domestic
contracts, post-separation adjustments, occupation rent, retroactivity, and
special and extraordinary expenses pursuant to
section 7
of the
Child Support
Guidelines, O. Reg. 391/97
as amended
(the
“Guidelines”
).

[
6
]

This trial was initially set for four to five days, later extended to
six days by the case management judge.  The trial expanded in scope and
length.  While the amount of time allocated was insufficient, in the end the
parties consumed a great deal more court time for various other reasons;  the trial
ended up being heard over sixteen days.

[
7
]

In March of 2022, just under two years after their agreed upon date of
separation, the parents signed a Separation Agreement, created using draft
obtained online from a website.  The father involved the child in creating a
handwritten parenting schedule that was attached as an appendix to it.  The body
of the Separation Agreement otherwise addresses parenting, child support and
the aforementioned property issue about the Thornhill Property.  Both parties would
later claim at this trial that they were under duress caused by the other, when
they signed the Separation Agreement.

[
8
]

At the outset of this trial, I was told that the parties were consenting
to set the Separation Agreement aside.  That consent was then immediately
withdrawn by the mother.  This led to or was interrelated with a disagreement
about whether the father, and later the mother, should be permitted to amend
his and her pleading to advance trust claims.  In addition, when this round of
the litigation began (this is the second case involving this family), the
father produced a surprise “Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement”.  The
authenticity of that document was hotly contested.  I was told that both
parties intended to call proposed experts about the authenticity of this
document;  in the end, only the mother would do so.  These intertwined
positions shifted and changed multiple times as the trial days unfolded.

[
9
]

I accept that the Separation Agreement is problematic as it concerns the
parenting and child support terms, especially in light of subsequent
developments.  I also recognize that the parties entered into the Separation
Agreement, on their own back in March of 2022, and there are inaccurate
statements in it about the exchange of financial disclosure and legal advice.
But I find that was very much their choice, and they knew what they were doing
when they negotiated its terms, especially insofar as its property terms are
concerned.   A wholesale attack on the Separation Agreement was unnecessary to
remedy the problems regarding parenting and child support.  The parties could
have simply had resort to
sections 56(1)
and
56(1.1)
of the
Family Law Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3
, as amended
.

[
10
]

Regarding the Thornhill Property, the parties agreed that the father
would buy out the mother’s interest in it, for $250,000.00.  Then, after
signing the Separation Agreement, for not good reasons, the parties proceeded
not to implement its property provisions.  The parties instead expanded the
issues at this trial a little over three years later for two simple reasons.
The mother wants to share in the current equity of the property, despite the
deal that she negotiated back in 2022.  The father, by contrast, wants to pay
her nothing (apart from perhaps refunding some contributions he said she made, amounting
to no more than 6 to 7 % of the current equity), despite the deal that he
negotiated.

[
11
]

What went on during this trial, with the Separation Agreement, and
earlier the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement, was troubling to the Court.
The father (and his sister) tried to deceive the Court.  Both parties
positioned and maneuvered.  The Court has no intention of enforcing the
Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement, which I find the mother did not sign. The
Court has no intention of enforcing the parties’ consent to set aside the
Separation Agreement either, nor does it intend to set its property terms aside
on the merits of the various duress and other related that the parties
pursued.
The Separation Agreement contains a
severability clause.  Even when the Court disregards the parenting and child
support terms under
sections 56(1)
and
(1.1)
of the
Family Law Act
,
the
property provisions do not fall.  The mother’s other claims for
post-separation adjustments and occupation rent are barred by the releases in
the Separation Agreement.  The appropriate remedy to address the father’s breach
of the Separation Agreement (i.e. the fact that he hasn’t paid the mother for
her interest in the Thornhill Property yet), is enforce the property terms in
it, order the property’s sale if the father does not comply, and award the
mother her claim for prejudgment interest.

[
12
]

The core problem respecting parenting is that the father has a serious
anger management problem.  He likely has an undiagnosed mental health disorder,
that has consequently gone untreated.   To be very clear right at the outset of
this Judgment, I find, despite the father’s arguments to the contrary, that this
was not a case of parental alienation.

[
13
]

The mother has admittedly made poor choices when entering into
relationships.  She has also behaved inappropriately at times, in her interactions
with the father, and regarding the manner that she has parented L., but I find
the latter to be related significantly to the impact that this relationship had
on her.  The mother was the victim of a number of incidents of family violence
perpetuated upon her by the father.  The violence was both verbal, and
physical.  The child has been exposed to his frightening family violence,
repeatedly.  Both parents have thrust the child into the middle of their
conflict, and ultimately this litigation, too.

[
14
]

So while it was common ground throughout this trial that both parents
love L., and L. loves both of her parents, in the end, things have gotten so
bad that L. is no longer willing to see her father outside of a supervised
setting, despite the therapeutic interventions that have been tried.  The reunification
therapist that became involved shortly before the start of this trial started characterized
the father’s conduct at a July 9, 2025 therapy session as abusive.  Following that
last therapy session, she essentially resigned.  The Court ended this trial
with concerns so serious, that it now worries the child cannot be shielded from
the father’s behaviour, including in a supervised setting.

[
15
]

All of which leaves the Court is in a very difficult position.  There
are very few remedial options left.  In this Judgment, I strive to balance the
child’s desire to continue to have some form of a relationship with the father,
but it has to be emotionally healthy.  The Court finds it must choose between
an outright termination of the father’s parenting time with L. recognizing that
will cause some harm to her, versus allowing some very limited and tightly
controlled contact, recognizing that may still cause some harm to her.  I find
that ordering anything else would pose a greater risk to this child than the
impact upon her, of limiting or terminating any father-daughter contact all
together, in these less than ideal circumstances.

[
16
]

This Court orders that there will be short, professionally supervised
video calls between the father and daughter, with very strict conditions.  If
the father misbehaves and either the child not longer wishes to attend, or the
supervisor no longer agrees to provide the service, then there will be in
effect no parenting time.  I am not making provision for the matter to be
returned to Court if that happens.  The fact that the father may derail these
visits is contemplated by the Court.  There will also be parallel provisions
requiring the father to address his behaviour and mental health, as
preconditions before he may seek to return the matter to court on a Motion to
Change.

[
17
]

Regarding child support, the parties agreed in their Separation
Agreement, that the father would pay the mother $500.00 per month commencing
April 1, 2022.  At this trial, the mother sought retroactive child support for
the period of time between April 3, 2020 and the March 2022 Separation
Agreement.  The mother claimed additional child support above that set out in
the Separation Agreement for the period April 1, 2022 to January 1, 2025, based
on various incomes that she would have the Court impute to the father, and a
set off calculation.  She claimed prospective child support in accordance with
the table, based on a change to the parenting arrangements after January 28,
2025, when the father’s parenting time was suspended and the child resumed
living with her primarily again.  To give effect to these claims, in her
written closing submissions, the mother asked the Court to impute hundreds of
thousands of dollars of income to the father in the years after the separation,
largely (but not entirely) based on various banking transactions extracted from
numerous pages of bank records.

[
18
]

The father initially claimed to be entitled to the repayment of an
overpayment of child support to the mother of about $50,000.00, for some period
between signing the Separation Agreement and now. That position was based on
the fact that the child was in a shared parenting arrangement, and he said, the
mother’s income was greater than his.  During his closing submissions, the father
then took no position about this.

[
19
]

Regardless of whether his claim for an overpayment was still being
pursued or not, the father failed to provide all of the disclosure needed to
determine properly his income.  The father did not in either his trial
affidavit sworn November 13, 2024 (the father’s “trial affidavit”) or during
his oral testimony, adduce the evidence needed to discharge his onus to prove
his income either.  To make matters worse, just as they distorted the truth
about the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement, the father (and his sister)
misrepresented the true state of affairs about the ownership of a marijuana
business that he started in late 2022, in an attempt to limit the income
generated from that business being attributed to him for the purposes of paying
child support.  With his written closing submissions, the father supplied an
excel spreadsheet/bank account analysis of one of his accounts only, for 2023
and 2024 only.  A number of the transactions on it, were unexplained.  During the
oral closing submissions, counsel said that if the Court imputed an income to
him from the marijuana business, at a level exceeding his positions about the
determination of his income, the father might just turn around and bring a
Motion to Change.

[
20
]

Despite the generous amount of trial time that was allocated, and
despite directions from the Court given at times to move on, the parties chose
to spend more time litigating the parenting issues and their challenges to the
two agreements, while allocating far less time to the income and child support
issues on their merits.  It is challenging for the Court to determine income
with precision under these circumstances, including when there was an end of
trial document dump, without all the specific questions about those documents being
asked.  Neither side assisted the Court to embark upon a proper analysis under

section 9
of the
Guidelines

either
,
even though there was a
shared parenting schedule in place either immediately, or soon after the
Separation Agreement, until early 2025.  There was likely inadequate evidence
called for the Court to deal with
section 9
properly, anyway
.

[
21
]

For the reasons that follow, I find the father is the real owner of the
marijuana business.  I  look to the limited and incomplete evidence I have
about that business (among other evidence), when drawing adverse inferences to
aid me to determine the father’s income  in for the years between 2022 and now.
I have decided to impute an income of $200,000.00 to the father.

[
22
]

I do not find that there should be child support ordered prior to the
Separation Agreement, because I do not find there to be a retroactive
entitlement covering that period.  Because of my income determination for the
father after that, and based on both parties’ failure to address
section 9

properly, I also do not find that there should be any additional child support,
or the repayment of an overpayment ordered, for any of the years that followed
the Separation Agreement, until early 2025.

[
23
]

The situation changes in 2025, not because of a change in the incomes,
but due to the change to the parenting schedule as of January 28, 2025.  I am therefore
ordering the father to pay child support to the mother for this child in the
amount of $1,659.00 per month, commencing February 1, 2025, based that imputed
income of $200,000.00.  There are new child support tables coming into effect
as of October 1, 2025.  The new amount of child support changes as of that
date, to $1,707.00 per month.  The father shall also pay his proportionate
share of the child’s
section 7
expenses commencing February 1, 2025.  The
percentage sharing is 60% (father) and 40% (mother).  I make provision below
for further limited submissions to aid me to quantify the
section 7
expenses
owing to the mother for the period February 1, 2025 until now.

PART II:        BACKGROUND
AND CONTEXT

A.

Background
Information About the Parties

[
24
]

The mother is from Columbia.  She came to Canada in October of 1999 and
has lived here since.  The mother’s educational background is in journalism,
but since coming to Canada she has worked for financial investment companies,
and now a major insurance company.

[
25
]

The father worked for years in the financial investment industry, both in
risk management and compliance, and providing investment advice.  In 2022, the
father lost his license to work in that industry, in which he had previously worked
for about two decades.  He lost his license because he engaged in an underhanded
transaction that was not disclosed to the regulatory body.  This was an act of
dishonesty, for which he was fined $40,000.00.  He is now self-employed as the
owner of a marijuana store.   The marijuana business is incorporated.  I was
told though, that the father’s sister owns the business.

[
26
]

The parties met at some point in 2007, when they both worked for a
particular financial company. At that time, the father was in a supervisory
role over the mother.  They were not then in a relationship.

[
27
]

The mother was previously in a relationship with a man named G.  They
separated in early 2010.  The mother has a child with G. named V., who is now
25 years old.  Following the mother’s separation from G., V. remained living
with her father and her grandparents in Milton, for a time.  V. now lives with
her mother, and L. There has been conflict between V. and the father.  I will
have more to say about this below.

[
28
]

Almost immediately after her relationship with G. ended, the mother
entered into another relationship with a friend of the father’s named F.  The
mother ended this relationship around the time she and the father became
intimate, and the mother became pregnant with L.  At times during this trial,
the father accused the mother of being promiscuous, using far more abusive and
derogatory language to do so, even though he was a participant in the affair,
too.

[
29
]

For his part, the father was previously married and divorced.  The
Thornhill Property is the home in which he used to reside with his former spouse.
In 2015, about three years into his cohabitation with the mother, the parties
jointly purchased the Thornhill Property.  I was told it had been purchased
from the father’s former wife’s parents.

B.

The
Mother’s Pregnancy with L. and the Change in the Nature of the Parties’
Relationship

[
30
]

The mother discovered that she was pregnant with L. during a trip home
to Columbia in December of 2011.     After her return from that trip to Columbia
in January of 2012, the mother started to stay during the week at the father’s
condominium.  The mother lost her job at some point, around the time of L.’s
birth, and she had no place to live.   The mother was contemplating returning
to Columbia but she didn’t, because the father asked her to move in.  It was
common ground that the two were living together fully, by November of 2012.

[
31
]

Both agreed that the father became involved during the mother’s
pregnancy.  The father described his attendance for L.’s birth as a special
memory.  He went on to recall other memories, such as when the child first
walked, when he first put the child to bed, and even a celebration the family
had together years later and post-separation, after L. got into her current,
private school.  But as I explain below, the father also tried to claim, at
times when discussing the property issues, that the relationship was not really
spousal.

C.

Background
Information About the Child, L.

[
32
]

The parents each spoke in positive terms when describing L., generally.
For example, in her trial affidavit sworn November 4, 2024 (the mother’s “trial
affidavit”), the mother described L. as “kind and loving”.  During her in court
testimony, she described L. as “amazing”.  The father testified that he has a
close relationship with L.  He said that she was his “life” and is “everything
to him”.

[
33
]

The mother testified that L. and her older sister V., have a good
relationship.  She described usual sibling conflict; nothing out of the
ordinary.  I understood that V. very much sees herself as L.’s big sister and
is protective in that sense.  L., however, has been exposed to V.’s and the
father’s conflict with one another.

[
34
]

By all accounts, L. loves basketball and she is a talented player.
Beginning in the 2024-2025 school year, L. now attends a private school that
has a focus on basketball.  The private school is expensive.  L. receives a
significant bursary, but it does not cover 100% of the fees.  Before she went
to this school, L. was in a Montessori school, and a French Immersion program.

[
35
]

Despite the high degree of conflict to which L. has been exposed for
years, by all accounts L. excels in school.  Amy de Munnik, the clinician who
assisted counsel for the Office of the Children’s Lawyer (the “OCL”), testified
that L. spoke positively about her school, both its academic component and its sports
component, at all times, across her multiple interviews.

[
36
]

L. is very programmed, but L. has been in the driver’s seat behind
having such an involved schedule.  The mother’s evidence was that she takes L.
to school by 7:45 AM.  L. has school between 8 AM and 2:30 PM each day.
Between 2:30 PM and 3:30 PM, L. participates in basketball practice for an
hour, followed by an hour of weight training or conditioning.  The mother said
she picks L. up around 4:45 PM.

[1]

[
37
]

L. has additional basketball practices on Mondays, Tuesdays and
Thursdays, between 7:30 PM to 9:00 PM on Mondays and Thursdays, and between
6:00 PM to 8:00 PM on Tuesdays, according to the mother.
[2]

L. is doing one-on-one personal training with former basketball players, on
Saturday mornings (from either 8:00 AM to 9:00 AM, or from 9:00 AM to 10:00
AM), and on Sunday evenings from 6:00 PM to 7:00 PM.  She does this on Sunday
evenings because the family attends church on Sunday mornings.

[
38
]

L. is in counselling with Adrienne Ambrosic.  Before that, she saw
Allison Gardiner.  Counselling started on a bi-weekly basis around June of
2024, following Himel J.’s Order of March 4, 2024 (see below).  L. switched
therapists from Ms. Gardiner to Ms. Ambrosic when L. started the private
school, as Ms. Gardner could not accommodate evening appointments.

[
39
]

The child’s therapy with Ms. Ambrosic typically occurred on alternate
Wednesdays or Fridays, after school, so that she did not miss practices.   The
child’s therapy stopped in April of 2025, right before the start of the trial.
By this point, reunification therapy had started (see below).  The mother said
Ms. Ambrosic was going to reach out after the trial, to see if therapy was to
resume.  On the last day of the trial during her Reply evidence, the mother
testified that L. resumed seeing Ms. Ambrosic on May 30, 2025.  I was told the
resumed sessions are weekly.  I also heard accusations during this trial, about
whether the father supported L.’s therapy and whether he delayed the signing of
Ms. Ambrosic’s retainer agreement, when the change over from Ms. Gardiner occurred.
This dispute no longer matters.

[
40
]

The child and the parents participated in reunification therapy with Lourdes
Geraldo following the Order of Himel J. dated March 27, 2025 (see below).  There
were a number of individual and joint sessions between April 26, 2025 and
mid-May, until the trial got underway, and then further sessions mid-trial as a
result of a direction I gave on June 27, 2025.  The process came to a halt when
the father had an explosive outburst during a therapy session on July 9, 2025, as
already indicated.

D.

The
Joint Purchase of the Thornhill Property in 2015 and the Alleged “Cohabitation
and Mortgage Agreement”

[
41
]

When the parties purchased the Thornhill Property in around June of 2015,
they took title jointly, and both are co-mortgagors.  Their accounts as to why
that was, were at odds.

[
42
]

In his trial affidavit, the father said that he was solely responsible
for the deposit, the down payment and closing fees.   He said that the mother
went on title purely so he could qualify for the mortgage.  He said that the
parties entered into the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement to protect his
financial interests in the event of a future separation.  During his
examination-in-chief, the father claimed that the mother had said to him at the
time, that she would never take a penny from him. Yet on March 18, 2022, the
parties signed their Separation Agreement, providing that the father would pay
the mother $250,000.00 to buy out her interest in the Thornhill Property.   The
reason the father now wants the Separation Agreement set aside, is so he can
rely on the more favourable terms in the alleged Cohabitation and Mortgage
Agreement, or irrespective of that, so he can claim sole ownership based on a
resulting trust.

[
43
]

The mother disputes the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement is a
legitimate document, saying it was fraudulently created.  She disputes that she
only went on title for financing purposes.  Rather she said that the parties
were planning on building a life together.
The mother referenced the
Separation Agreement in her Application dated January 13, 2024.  She did not
refer to the existence of any other domestic contract.

[
44
]

The relevant terms of the alleged Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement
are:

(a)

The
document states that the parties are not married or in a common law
relationship and are not intending on getting married;

(b)

The
document states that the mother was put on title to the Thornhill Property, and
on the mortgage, for financing purposes only;

(c)

The
document states that the father is the “rightful and sole owner” of the
Thornhill Property.  It goes on to say that the father is responsible for all
carrying costs, maintenance and repairs, and for renovations to the Thornhill
Property, but the mother will pay for utility bills while living there;

(d)

The
document states that if the Thornhill Property is ever sold, the father will
receive the proceeds;

(e)

The
document states that it is “irrevocable and cannot be terminated”; and

(f)

The
document also states that both parties acknowledge that they had an opportunity
to seek independent legal advice before entering into it, and they understand
its implications.

E.

The
Post-Separation Residential Arrangements

[
45
]

Following their agreed upon date of separation of April 3, 2020, the
father continued to live in the Thornhill Property.  The Thornhill Property has
generated rental income from a basement apartment in it in the years since the
separation, until very recently.

[
46
]

The mother said in her trial affidavit that although she moved out, she returned
to the Thornhill property “occasionally” to clean and to make sure L. was
comfortable, as the child reported the house was quite dirty.  It is common
ground that she did this, and it appears to me that she did this more than
“occasionally”.  The mother said that she stopped doing this sometime in July
of 2023 due to the father’s “continuous abuse”.  In his trial affidavit, the
father claimed that the purpose behind the mother returning to the Thornhill
Property was to “gather evidence” to use against him.  That comment probably
stems, at least in part, from the fact that the mother took a number of
photographs depicting the appalling, messy and dirty state of the Thornhill
Property, that the father was living in after the mother moved out, and in
which L. was having visits with her father.

[
47
]

The mother has been living in rental accommodations more or less since
the separation.  Until the parties signed the Separation Agreement, L. lived
with her mother primarily.  There was a tenant subletting a room there, too,
for a time.  According to the mother, she was unable to afford the rental
otherwise.

[
48
]

After the Separation Agreement dated March 18, 2022, there was a shared
parenting arrangement in place.  While the written version of the parenting
schedule in the body of the Separation Agreement had the child in the mother’s
primary care, the calendar attached to it as an appendix actually depicted a
shared schedule.  It was disputed as to whether that was the case in the
original iteration of the appendix, or whether it was modified a few months
later to reflect the shared schedule.  Although the mother’s child support
calculations attached as a schedule to her written closing submissions say
there was a shared parenting schedule immediately after the Separation
Agreement, the father’s position was that it only started in June of 2022, not
right away.  In the end, when the shared parenting schedule started doesn’t
really matter.  I will have more to say about how this shared parenting
schedule was put in place, what happened while the parents’ operated under it,
and what its impact should be on the child support claims, below.

[
49
]

Since January 28, 2025, L. resides exclusively with her mother again, as
indicated already.  I address why that is, later on, too.

[
50
]

Except for her sister who resides in Ontario, the majority of the
mother’s extended family live abroad.  This includes L.’s maternal grandmother,
who lives in Columbia.  But there were factual disputes at this trial about how
frequently the maternal grandmother comes to Canada, and about how long she
stays once she gets here.  As such, I heard evidence from the mother, her
sister, the maternal grandmother, the father and his sister, and certain
documentary evidence, about these matters.

[
51
]

The marginal relevance of this seemed to be threefold.  I heard some
evidence about whether the maternal grandmother pays rent to her daughter while
here (she does not).  The father complained that the mother does not have
sizeable enough accommodations for each of herself, L. and V., when the
grandmother visits.  He and his sister also alleged that the maternal
grandmother is abusive to L., because she engages in body shaming her, just
like she did with her own daughters.

[
52
]

Regarding the second complaint about the size of the mother’s
accommodations, the mother and the child share a bedroom when the grandmother
visits.  This case does not turn on that.  The fact that the father raised this
reveals some lack of insight on his part when it comes to his own behaviour
regarding the financial issues (i.e. not implementing the property terms in the
Separation Agreement, and stopping paying child support).  The fact the mother
then had to respond to this complaint, by calling her mother and introducing
travel records, wasted trial time.

[
53
]

The body shaming allegation was another area about which I heard
evidence, disproportionate to its import.  This is another matter upon which
this case is not going to turn.  The child has not raised this as an issue of
concern.  It was disputed as to whether it has even occurred
vis a vis

the child.  Quite ironically, while complaining that L. has been subjected to
“body shaming” by the grandmother, and even though at one time he expressed
concern about the manner in which he said the maternal grandmother had treated

]

The

At a

The

The

[

In his trial affidavit, the father described the circumstances

]

]

During her examination-in-chief, the mother denied that she had ever

[
84
]

[6]

[
85
]

voir dire
regarding these photographs.  The
mother testified that she had taken them soon after the incident had occurred,
but was uncertain precisely when.  She testified that she had not altered them
in any way, and then sent them to her sister for safekeeping.

[
86
]

A witness is not required to remember with complete precision when the
photographs were taken.  I was satisfied on the
voir dire
that the
mother had taken these photographs contemporaneously with the events in
question, and that they accurately depicted the damage the father had caused.  The
father himself admitted right in his trial affidavit, to having damaged the
laptop, yet he objected to the admissibility of photographs that showed the

87
]

During the

88
]

89
]

I find on a balance of probabilities that the mother’s account of this
incident of violence is more likely than the father’s, for the following
reasons:

(a)

The
father has an admitted anger management problem.  Even if the mother was
insisting on addressing an issue and he was trying to be “avoidant” as he
claimed, he was unable to regulate his emotions;

(b)

Regarding
the mother’s testimony that L. heard her father screaming in the shower, I do

(c)

The
father revealed throughout this trial that he is fixated on the mother’s
alleged sexual behaviour;

(d)

The
mother denied having ever destroyed either of V.’s or L’s belongings.  She was
not impugned on cross-examination on this point; and

(e)

Whereas
the father himself admitted to breaking the mother’s work laptop computer.  The
photographs that the mother tendered also reveal this, in particular the
serious extent to which he caused this damage.

[
90
]

Whether or not she witnessed the entire affair or only part of it, it is

mother was either kicked out of, or basically had to leave the house.
L.
was 7 years old at the time
.

[
100
]

There
was conflict between the parents about the father’s telephone contact with L.

Anyways! You
lie so much just like your fat ugly butch
(sic.
) cousin! Ou
(sic.
)
Colombiana whores! lying slut!
🖕
[i.e.
middle finger, meaning “fuck you”]

and your mama!

101
]

I
find the following:

(a)

The
parties agreed to the trip;

(b)

The father
paid for the tickets and even planned at one point to travel there himself, but
that did not materialize;

(c)

While
various government documents outlining the changing travel restrictions in
place during this period could have been put before the Court (to either

notable to me is that the parties agreed to this travel, during the Covid-19

(d)

Even if
she did manipulate the father (which I do not find), I am left wondering what
impact that actually has on the current conundrum that confronts the Court and
the decision that I must make.  This trip occurred
between 4 and 4.5 years
ago
.

[
102
]

What
this evidence revealed is the extent to which the father is fixated on this
history.  He even said in his trial affidavit, that he has resentment towards
the mother that he is still “actively working to process and accept
to this
date
” [my emphasis added].  I do not agree that this trip is the reason for
the parents’ dysfunction, or the father’s reckless, irritable, reactive and
impulsive behaviour.  The reality is this relationship was already conflictual
and dysfunctional, well before the Columbia trip occurred. The father’s
reckless, irritable, reactive and impulsive behaviour very likely stems from other
causes.  Regardless, the mother’s Columbia Trip is not a credible explanation
or a reasonable justification for the behaviour.

]

incident was described in one of several paragraphs in the mother’s trial

(a)

(b)

Regardless

his lack of parenting skills; and

(c)

The child
was 9 years old
when this incident occurred.

]

L.

The
Christmas Incident, 2024, and Its Aftermath

[
187
]

What
happened during the Christmas holiday in 2024, after the November 2024 trial
didn’t’ proceed, was very much talked about during this trial.  I heard about
it from each of the parents, from Ms. Gadsen, from Ms. de Munnik, from Ms.
Geraldo, and from the father’s sister, during their examinations-in-chief and
in cross-examinations.  The Christmas incident was another example of an
incident, like those which occurred in February 2018 and March 2022, that
involved V. (and other family members), in the conflict and chaos.

[
188
]

The
Court’s impression after hearing a great deal of evidence about the Christmas incident,
was that it was a significant, alarming, upsetting and disturbing incident, for
which all those who were involved are responsible.  The arguments raised in
this case included ones about fairness to the father, and about the extent to
which the fallout from the Christmas incident impacted the trajectory of this
case.  While I continue to hold that view about who was responsible, counsel
for the mother characterized the incident differently, as “the straw that broke
the camel’s back”, during closing submissions.  That is a better descriptor.
What happened is as follows.

(1)

The
Exit-Pre Trial Before Bennett J. on December 2, 2024

[
189
]

The
Christmas incident began with an exit pre-trial before Bennett J. on December
2, 2024 that was held in an attempt to settle this case after the November 2024
trial did not proceed.  The only thing that got resolved, was the division of the
Christmas holiday break, for 2024 only.  I could neither locate an Endorsement
for this event, nor did the parties file one, but it is not contested terrain
that the parties entered into Interim Minutes of Settlement that day.  Their
agreement then unraveled before the ink was even dry on the consent document.

[
190
]

The
Interim Minutes of Settlement provided that L. was to be with the mother on
Christmas Eve from 6 PM until Christmas Day on 8 PM.  As it happened, Christmas
Eve fell on a Tuesday, which according to the regular schedule would have been
one of the father’s overnight parenting days.  Christmas Day, a Wednesday, was
one of the mother’s overnight parenting days under the regular schedule.
Because the Interim Minutes otherwise say the parties were to follow the
current schedule for the balance of the break, the mother took the position at
this trial, that the Interim Minutes of Settlement meant that the child would
come into her care on Christmas Eve (i.e. Tuesday, during the father’s
parenting time), stay with her overnight until Wednesday at 8 PM, and because the
next parenting exchange wasn’t until Thursday, the child would remain with her
overnight on Christmas Day, despite the reference to 8PM.  That too, is how I
read the document as drafted.

[
191
]

The
father took the position at trial that the child ought to have been with him
overnight on Christmas Day into Boxing Day, even though that is not what the
document said.  To make this point, he claimed that Bennett J. said otherwise at
the exit pre-trial, and accused Ms. Yehia of sharp practice and deliberately
mis-drafting the document.   To quote specifically what the father rudely,
sarcastically and inappropriately said about Bennett J. during Ms. Yehia’s
cross-examination when accusing Ms. Yehia of inappropriate conduct:

Like is Justice Bennett retarded that he would say
drop her off at 8:00 o’clock and then start the regular schedule.

[
192
]

As explained in more detail later, the father brought
a mid-trial motion to get access to the transcript of the exit pre-trial, not
for the purposes of challenging the mother’s credibility and proving exactly
what the agreement was supposed to be, but because he asserted that there had
been some discussion about the pleadings issue that was relevant to whether leave
at trial should be granted to amend.  As there was a live issue at trial about
amending the pleadings, I ordered production of the transcript for that purpose
only, while saying the parties were to provide me with a redacted transcript,
so as to not disclose improper settlement discussions to the trial judge.  Once
he was armed with the transcript, the father’s request to use the transcript
expanded, to show what exactly the Christmas agreement was supposed to be.  I
did not allow that for oral reasons.

Of note, there was a signed document that sets out
what the agreement was, and both parties were represented when they settled the
division of time over the Christmas break, the mother by Ms. Yehia, and the
father by his second lawyer, Ms. Licata.   Two lawyers were involved in this
negotiation; even if Ms. Yehia drafted it, the father had counsel with whom to
review the document.

(2)

The
Events of Christmas Day, 2024

[
193
]

Despite
the parties’ differing statements about what the agreement was supposed to be,
the parties did not follow either of their alleged understandings as to its
terms.  The mother testified that a mere seven days later on December 9, 2024,

December 25.  The mother said she told the child that wasn’t correct, but then proceeded
to ask her what she wanted to do, regardless of the Interim Minutes of
Settlement.  According to the mother, the child said that she did not want to
sleep over at her father’s house, but didn’t mind spending “a little bit more
time with daddy”.

[
194
]

Next,
the mother initiated written communications with the father to propose a
different schedule for the Christmas holiday.  For example, the mother testified
that she proposed the father could keep L. a bit later on Christmas Eve, and
that the father could also see the child for about 1 hour between 7 PM and 8 PM
on Christmas Day.  While she testified that she followed up with him two or
three times, there was never a response from him.

[
195
]

The
father then involved the child directly, rather than dealing with the mother.  The

[
196
]

mother testified that at 7:30 PM, L. called her, to confirm what time she would

197
]

[
198
]

mother testified that some of the calls she made did not get answered.  One

199
]

]

Whether

There
is no general principle that prevents a judge on a best interests’ analysis
from considering the actions of a child protection agency:  see
B.J.T. v.
J.D.,
2022 SCC 24
¶63.
A court order conferring upon the Society the power
to suspend parenting time is unusual, particularly when it is made outside the
parameters of a child protection proceeding and its governing legislation.  The

went into the Society’s decision-making prior to suspending the father’s

protection application at different points in time after the suspension.   The

[

]

This
trial is not an appeal about the correctness of Himel J.’s Order.  Furthermore:

(a)

Although
the father claimed that the August 9, 2024 was made without his consent, that

Quite

and

M.

Findings
and Conclusions About the Christmas Incident and Its Aftermath

[
248
]

The
father sees himself as the victim of this incident.  From his perspective, the
mother is the one who behaved badly on Christmas day; he was the one who
eventually de-escalated the situation. The Society (and the OCL) launched
“flawed” or “one-sided” and “biased” investigations, according to him. He believes
he has been treated unfairly.

[
249
]

Even
if I were to find that the mother, or the mother and V. were entirely
responsible, the fact remains that from the child’s perspective, the relationship
with the father is fractured, and the Christmas incident is not the sole
contributing cause of that.  The father’s perspective is disconnected to the
years of conflict, explosive outbursts and even physical violence that he
engaged in.   For this reason, I tend to agree with Ms. Yehia’s closing
submission, that the Christmas incident is probably better described as the
proverbial “straw that broke the camel’s back”, as opposed to a stand-alone
incident that altered the trajectory of this case.

[
250
]

As
far as I am concerned, both parents, V. and the father’s sister, each bear
responsibility here.  All four contributed to the conflict, in different ways.
The three adults who testified at this trial, demonstrated a lack of insight
into the ways that their actions contributed to the problems, as they talked
about the Christmas incident and its aftermath, repeatedly in Court.  Each one
of them lost sight of the fact that L.,
who was 12 years old at the time
,
sat there and watched the whole thing unfold, to the point that L. jumped out
in the physical defense of her mother.  The problematic behaviour continued
after the Christmas incident was over.

[
251
]

In
summary, my findings about the Christmas incident and its aftermath are:

(a)

There
was an agreement signed earlier in December, which was not followed;

(b)

The father
should not have involved the child in trying to change the terms of the Interim
Minutes of Settlement;

(c)

The mother
should not have then engaged in a scheduling discussion;

(d)

I do
not believe that the father was unaware as to the reason that the mother
dropped the child off on Christmas day;

(e)

After
the mother sat on the driveway for a while and L. did not come out, the mother
could have just left, to avoid the escalation.  She, at least, acknowledged
this during cross-examination;

(f)

V.
should not have attended on the scene.  Her past encounters with the father
have not gone well;

(g)

To the
father’s credit, he was somewhat calm when he came out, eventually (although
not entirely – I heard evidence that he yelled at his sister to leave).  And
while he eventually put L. in the car to leave,  he was also the one who had
first created the potential for this dispute and he put the child in the middle
in the process, starting back on December 9;

(h)

On his
own admission, the father even re-involved the child in scheduling discussions
again, on December 25 itself.  And so yes, while in the moment on the evening
of December 25 he eventually came outside “calm” (somewhat), he did so in a
situation that he played a great role in creating.  And he only came out after
he first tried to tell the mother that L. would be staying overnight, and then
he stopped taking her calls;

(i)

After
all was said and done, in January, the father tried to leverage and exploit the
situation for his advantage in these proceedings, to the detriment of his
relationship with the child;

(j)

The
father lacked some insight when he testified about the Christmas incident and
its aftermath.  In cross-examination, the father was asked whether he thought
his conduct had any part in L. asking for the suspension.  The father said no;

(k)

The
father deliberately breached the Order of Himel J. of March 27, 2025 by
attending the basketball game.  Like so many other incidents, the situation
escalated.  The police were called;

(l)

The
father’s sister was an incredible witness, not just about the Christmas incident,
but also about her subsequent interaction with L. and regarding the marijuana
business, discussed later.  She tried to give me an incredible explanation for

PART VII:     ISSUES AND ANALYSIS RESPECTING THE VALIDITY OF THE COHABITATION
AND MORTGAGE AGREEMENT AND THE SEPARATION AGREEMENT

A.

Applicable Legal Principles Concerning Deference to Domestic Contracts

[
334
]

In

Anderson v. Anderson,
2023 SCC 13
,
the parties signed a simple
Separation Agreement, which essentially provided that each party would keep the
property held in their name and gave up all rights to the other’s property,
except for the family home and household goods.  The agreement had been
prepared by the wife, and signed at a meeting with two friends as witnesses.  There
was no financial disclosure between the parties, and neither had the benefit of
independent legal advice before signing it.  Nearly 17 months after the wife
petitioned for divorce, the husband counter-petitioned and sought corollary
relief, arguing that the agreement was signed without legal advice and under
duress.

[
335
]

Although
this case was dealt with under Saskatchewan’s legislation, and although one of
the issues before the Court was whether the framework in
Miglin v. Miglin,

2003 SCC 24

applied (it did not strictly apply), the Supreme Court
articulated the following principles, or policy objectives behind paying
deference to domestic contracts, at ¶ 33:

(a)

The
proper interpretive framework for assessing a domestic contract is
statute-specific;

(b)

Useful
principles still emerge from
Miglin
and subsequent jurisprudence;

(c)

Domestic
contract should generally be encouraged and supported by courts, within the
bounds permitted by the legislature, absent a compelling reason to discount the
agreement;

(d)

Deference
flows from the recognition that self-sufficiency, autonomy and finality are
important objectives in the family law context;

(e)

The
parties are better placed than courts to understand what is fair within the
context of their relationship; and

(f)

The
private resolution of family affairs outside the adversarial process avoid the
costs and tumult of protracted litigation.

[
336
]

The
Supreme Court went on to find at ¶ 34 that balanced against those principles, courts
should recognize that negotiations take place in a “singularly challenging
environment, often at a time of acute emotional stress, in which one or both of
the parties may be particularly vulnerable”.  Judges should balance contractual
autonomy and certainty, with concerns of fairness, sensitive to the
vulnerabilities that can arise in the family law context, but without presuming
that spouses lack agency because of the stressful context in which negotiations
occur.

[
337
]

At
¶ 35-37, and 42 the Supreme Court wrote that concerns about vulnerabilities may
be countered by the presence of procedural safeguards, including full and frank
disclosure and professional assistance.  The rigor of a court’s review of a
domestic contract though, depends on the statute.  Under Ontario’s legislation,
there are minimum requirements that a domestic contract must be in writing,
signed by the parties and witnessed:  see
section 55(1)
of the
Family Law
Act
.
Beyond that, in general a court will look at the circumstances surrounding
the contract’s execution and the substance of the agreement, where authorized
by the legislation, and by reference to the governing legislative regime.  The
purposes and criteria of the governing statute provide an objective yardstick
against which to assess the parties’ subjective understanding of what is fair,
and they limit the risk that parties will depart significantly from public
policy goals expressed by the legislature.

B.

Analysis Concerning Whether the Parties’ Consent to Set Aside the
Separation Agreement Should Be Enforced

[
338
]

In
this case, the parties’ challenges to the Separation Agreement do not rest
solely on the grounds for setting aside or disregarding domestic contracts provided
for in the
Children’s Law Reform Act

and the
Family Law Act
.
Prior
to trial, the parties through correspondence between counsel, wrote to each
other saying they were content to set aside the Separation Agreement.  The
mother then withdrew her consent at the outset of the trial.  Although at one
point the mother framed the reasons for so doing as being to preserve her
ability to launch an alternative argument (i.e. she wanted to be able to rely
on the Separation Agreement if the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement is found

understanding that the father would not be launching a resulting trust claim.  Now

[
339

Adding
to this complexity (and what I find to be both sides’ positioning and

(1)

The
Disingenuous Shifting Positions and Maneuvering

[
340

articulated in

Anderson v. Anderson
. Both sides engaged in this.

i.

The Mother’s Pleading

[

The

and
56(1.1)
of

The father

]

]

th

[
349
]

On
June 19, 2025, while the trial was on its first hiatus following the illness, the

[
350
]

There
was then yet another discussion about the amendment issue at the outset of June

[
351
]

On
June 25, 2025, the father finally tendered a formal Notice of Motion and a

[
352
]

In
my written ruling dated July 14, 2025 dismissing the father’s recusal/mistrial

[
353
]

The
elusive 14B Motion of the father’s, dated July 3, 2025, was processed by court

Perhaps that changed in anticipation of what the mother would later try to do
(i.e. argue unjust enrichment).

[
354
]

On
the last day of trial, the mother filed a Notice of Cross-Motion dated July 18,
2025, asking to amend the mother’s pleadings, to claim various alternative Orders.
The proposed amendments included a claim that the mother is the beneficial
owner of the Thornhill Property as a result of a joint family venture.

[
355
]

There
was a separate set of shifting and maneuvering during this trial that went on
concerning the proposed expert evidence about the validity of the Cohabitation
and Mortgage Agreement, too.  This is discussed in some detail below, when I
address the validity of that document on its merits.

[
356
]

What
the correspondence establishing the consent to set the Separation Agreement
aside established (once I eventually saw it) was that on November 28, 2024, the
father’s second lawyer, Ms. Licata, wrote to Ms. Yehia, and said that the
father would agree to set the Separation Agreement aside.  She proposed this
“in order to avoid lengthening the trial with examinations and
cross-examination on this particular issue”.  She wrote this even though
current counsel both said they still wanted to call evidence about the
Separation Agreement, and in the end, the consent would achieved the exact opposite
of creating efficiencies.

[
357
]

On
May 6, 2025, Ms. Yehia wrote to Mr. Sheena asking him to confirm whether the
father was still in agreement that the Separation Agreement be set aside.

[
358
]

On
May 9, 2025, Mr. Sheena said that the father was agreeable, but he still
intended to rely on it “as an evidentiary document”.

[
359
]

Regarding
the amendment motions, the father claimed that it was clear throughout that he
intended to proceed this way, as already indicated.  In her written closing
submissions, the mother/her counsel attempted to argue that the mother would have
presented her case differently, by calling the real estate lawyer who handled
the purchase of the Thornhill Property to testify, had the pleading been
clear.  Yet she made this submission after having already given evidence
herself, and having already cross-examined the father on some of the real
estate documents that would have been in that lawyer’s file.  I heard all sorts
of evidence and commentary from both sides or counsel, about what the intention
was at the time the property was acquired, and what various terms on real
estate documents that he signed meant.  I also heard much evidence from the
mother, relative to her argument that the parties were in a joint family
venture.

(2)

Applicable
Legal Principles Concerning the Enforceability of Settlements Through Lawyers’
Correspondence During Pending Litigation

[
360
]

Unhelpfully,
neither side then made many submissions respecting the enforceability of their
consent to set the Separation Agreement aside, achieved through lawyers’
correspondence, or about the Court’s discretion not to enforce that consent.

[
361
]

It
is well established that a lawyer can bind his or her client to settle pending
proceedings, through correspondence:  see
Scherer v. Paletta,
1966 CanLII 286 (ON CA)
,
[1966] 2 O.R.
524 (C.A.)
;
see
Geropolous v. Geropolous,
1982 CanLii 2020
(Ont.
C.A.)
;
see also
Lindsay v. Lindsay,
2021 ONSC 4674
(S.C.J.)
, aff’d by

2021 ONSC 7085
(Div. Ct.) ¶
35-36
.

[
362
]

The
Court nevertheless retains a narrow discretion not to enforce the terms of such
a settlement achieved by lawyer’s letters.  The exercise of that discretion is
reserved, especially where the settlement has been partially or fully
performed, to rare cases where compelling circumstances establish that
enforcement is not in the interests of justice:  see
Srebot v. Srebot Farms
Ltd.,
2013 ONCA 84
¶
6
.

[
363
]

Milos v. Zagras,
1998 CanLii 7119
(Ont. C.A.)

concerned one such rare situation, where the settlement had been
entered into on the basis of a mistake.  In that case the mistake concerned what
the settlement instructions had been.  The Ontario Court of Appeal added as
factors to consider in the analysis:

(a)

where no order giving effect to the settlement
has been taken out, the fact that the parties’ pre-settlement positions remain
intact;

(b)

apart from losing the benefit of the impugned
settlement, whether the respondent will be prejudiced (or not) if the
settlement is not enforced;

(c)

the degree to which the applicant would be
prejudiced if judgment is granted in relation to the prejudice that the
respondent would suffer if the settlement is not enforced; and

(d)

the fact that no third parties were, or would
be, affected if the settlement is not enforced.

(3)

Findings
and Conclusions Respecting Whether the Consent to Set the Separation Agreement
Aside Should be Enforced

[
364
]

For
the reasons set out next, I find as follows regarding the consent to set the
Separation Agreement aside:

(a)

Assuming without necessarily needing to decide that the parties did in
fact unequivocally consent to set aside the Separation Agreement through
lawyer’s correspondence prior to trial while this case was pending, this is one
of those rare instances in which the Court will not enforce such a settlement,
if it was in fact unequivocally achieved;

(b)

It is true that trust claims were not pleaded by either side.  It is
also true that the father signaled his intent to amend prior to the trial,
several times.  But it is also true, that Himel J. denied leave to amend at
least twice prior to trial;

(c)

There was an unfortunate inconsistency in the pre-trial Endorsements.  On
the one hand, notwithstanding the complaints I heard at this trial about the
need to amend, and the counter complaints about the lack of notice,
both
parties
listed “Trust claims – jointly owned property” as an issue for
trial that each intended to pursue, in their list of triable issues on the
Trial Scheduling Endorsement Form.  But the manner in which the Trial
Scheduling Endorsement Form was finalized in case management was chaotic as
described already, caused by the father not following a practice direction
about preparation of the form for the Trial Scheduling Conference, or an Order
of this Court.  I heard no evidence that the parties even alerted Himel J. to
this inconsistency, when she approved the Trial Scheduling Endorsement Form in
these chaotic circumstances, after she had previously been asked to grant leave
to amend pleadings and denied it;

(d)

So on the other hand, because of the inconsistency, I am prepared to
accept the mother’s counsel’s argument, and give her the benefit of the doubt, that
the mother’s offer to set aside the Separation Agreement was made in the
context of a case where trust claims were not pleaded, and would not be pleaded.
There was an argument to be made, that the mother was entitled to rely on Himel
J.’s earlier Endorsement denying leave to amend, which was never appealed or
set aside;

(e)

Although perhaps its use as an “evidentiary document” would have been straightforward
had the Separation Agreement been set aside at the outset of the trial, setting
it aside might have also lead to even further arguments, objections and confusion,
in this instance about the use to which that document could have then been legitimately
put, during the trial;

(f)

No order has been taken out giving effect to the settlement to set the
Separation Agreement aside; and

(g)

Third parties are not affected one way or the other.

[
365
]

Regarding
the prejudice analysis, I have concerns about both parties’ approaches taken
during this trial.  Both parties’ ultimate goal, in trying to get the
Separation Agreement set aside, was to obtain an improper financial advantage
to the detriment of the other.  I am troubled by this, especially in light of
my findings (below), adverse to the father, that the Cohabitation and Mortgage
Agreement is not a genuine document, and that it was tendered by him to deceive
the Court in furtherance of that goal to obtain improper financial advantage.  His
request to amend to raise trust claims, whether framed as an alternative or
additional argument, was advanced in the same vein, to hedge his bets if his
attempt to rely on the domestic contract that he manufactured, had  failed.  I
am equally troubled by this in light of my findings (below), adverse to both
parties, that they knew full well what they were bargaining for, when they
signed the Separation Agreement, especially insofar as the property provisions in
it are concerned.

[
366
]

Given
these findings then, it is hard for me to reconcile why the Court would still
just turn a blind eye, and enforce the parties’ consent, even more so when that
consent was negotiated in an uncertain environment as to the state of affairs
regarding the pleadings.

[
367
]

Recently
in
Martin v. 11037315 Canada Inc.,
2025 ONCA 648
,
the Ontario Court of
Appeal refused to accept a consent to set aside a Judgment on appeal, where
that was sought for an improper purpose.  At ¶ 18, the Court wrote, “[t]his
case highlights the mischief that can occur if this court were simply to rubber
stamp an agreement between parties to allow an appeal on consent”.  In seeking
to proceed in this fashion, the parties were asking the appellate court to
“whitewash” a finding of misconduct without any basis for doing so.  To do so,
would bring the administration of justice into disrepute:  see ¶ 19.

[
368
]

While
I appreciate the context before me is different, in that the parties were not
trying to set aside a Judgment or findings previously made, as a matter of
policy, deference is supposed to be paid to valid agreements.  To enforce this
consent and unravel the Separation Agreement in its entirety, based on counsel’s
correspondence here, runs counter to those policy objectives in my view.  It
also runs counter to what the Court is supposed to achieve when applying the
Family
Law Rules,
namely to reduce conflict and settle cases, or when people have
to go to trial, to narrow the scope of those trials.

[
369
]

I
recognize, as Price J. wrote at ¶ 39 and 30 of
Davis v. Hutchinson,
2011
ONSC 2248
,
that resolving a dispute by negotiation offers distinct
advantages to litigants over resolving it by a contested hearing.  It normally
results in costs savings, and in the family law context it can often do less
damage to the litigants’ relationships with each other and with the
children.     Had the parties consented to set aside the Separation Agreement
because they had negotiated something else that would be one thing.
[12]

But the effect of enforcing the consent to set the Separation Agreement here achieves
none of the benefits that Price J. identified in
Davis v. Hutchison.
Rather
it encourages or promotes the opposite.

[
370
]

The
consent to set the Separation Agreement aside is tied up and intertangled with an
onslaught of other claims.  In other words, the prospect that the Court might
give effect to the consent to set aside the Separation Agreement contributed to
the expansion of the scope and complexity of this trial, not its reduction or
narrowing.   I am left querying whether the policy principles in
Anderson v.
Anderson

are such that perhaps litigants should be disallowed to consent to
set aside otherwise valid domestic contracts, when to do so has such a
detrimental impact on the administration of justice, as it did in this case.

[
371
]

Regardless,
I would also point out that the consent to set the Separation Agreement aside
is of course intertwined with the Separation Agreement itself.  Returning to
the Ontario Court of Appeal’s comments in
Milos v. Zagras
,
there has
been part performance of some of the financial terms of the Separation
Agreement, specifically the father’s payment of $10,000.00.  The father even
admitted during his testimony, that he thought this term for the payment to the
mother of $10,000.00 was “fair”.  In other words, this is a case of part
performance, not of the lawyer’s consent itself, but of the underlying
document.  The consent, if enforced, would unravel that term, which has been
performed, leading to yet another issue, about how to credit that payment.  That
too militates in favour of not enforcing the consent.

[
372
]

For
these reasons, I decline to enforce the consent to set aside the Separation
Agreement reached between counsel.

C.

The Parties’ Positions Regarding the Validity of the Cohabitation
and Mortgage Agreement

[
373
]

The
parties’ positions about the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement are simple, when
considered in isolation from the other related claims and arguments.  The
mother’s position is that the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement is a
fraudulent document.   The father claimed otherwise, and said that he entered
into the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement, to protect his financial
interests in the event of a separation.

[
374
]

In
an  attempt to bolster his arguments about the validity of the Cohabitation and
Mortgage Agreement, the father also said the following three things in his
trial affidavit:

(a)

The father said that after discussing with the mother, the financial
arrangements for the purchase of the property, the parties then operated their
finances in a manner consistent with the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement;

(b)

The
father said that his expert’s report opines that the Cohabitation and Mortgage
Agreement is a genuine document; and

(c)

The father said that the mother misrepresented facts through these
proceedings, including those centered around the validity of the Separation
Agreement.

[
375
]

The
father proved neither (a) or (b) at this trial.  There were problems with both
sides’ evidence and arguments about the Separation Agreement, not just the
mother’s.  But the mother’s evidence about the Cohabitation and Mortgage
Agreement was credible, and the father’s (and his sister’s) evidence about it,
was not.

D.

Findings and Conclusions Regarding the Validity of the
Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement

[
376
]

On
a balance of probabilities, I find:

(a)

The father failed to prove that the mother went on title only for financing
purposes;

(b)

The father tailored his evidence to try to create the illusion that the
parties followed the terms of the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement that he
made up, to bolster his argument that it is a genuine document.  He also
tailored his evidence to minimize some of the inconvenient evidence about the
parties’ subsequent financial contributions to the Thornhill Property to
bolster the strength of his request to amend and his resulting trust arguments;

(c)

The Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement is not a genuine document;

(d)

The father created this document to try to use it in this lawsuit to
gain a financial advantage;

(e)

The Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement was not signed by both parties, and
witnessed, as required by
section 55(1)
of the
Family Law Act
;

(f)

The father’s attempt to use a not genuine document was part of his role
in the shifting positions and maneuvering, described above;

(g)

It was also an attempt by him, to deceive the Court; and

(h)

As explained below, even if I am mistaken about the authenticity of the
Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement, the parties later bargained for a
different property settlement in the Separation Agreement.

[
377
]

I
make these findings for the following reasons.

(1)       The Mother Did Not Go on Title Only For Financing
Purposes and the Parties Did Not Follow Its Terms

[
378
]

The
father failed to prove that the mother went on title to the Thornhill Property only
for financing purposes is.  He contradicted himself about this.  For example,
on June 24, 2025, the father testified that he funded the purchase of the
property with his savings.  On June 25, 2025, he claimed that he could not
qualify for the mortgage in part because of the condominium that he then owned,
but earlier he had testified that he would later sell it.  He testified at
another time that he used the condominium’s sale proceeds to fund some
renovations to the property. But the renovations occurred almost immediately
after the purchase of the residence.

[
379
]

The
father did not tender any documents or other evidence (apart from his own say
so) to corroborate his inability to arrange for financing without the mother,
nor for example about whether he could have qualified for bridge financing
pending the sale of the condominium.  He even admitted in cross-examination on
July 15, 2025, that he didn’t try to qualify for the mortgage on his own,
although he tried to explain this away, by professing he knew what the outcome
would be.

[
380
]

Regarding
his claim the parties operated their finances subsequently in a manner
consistent with the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement, they did not.  The
father’s claim that he covered all subsequent financial contributions
“exclusively” except for utilities when the two were living together is not
correct.  In her trial affidavit, the mother said that the plan after the
purchase, was for the father to pay the mortgage, and she would cover the
utilities, home insurance, and the family’s other expenses, as well as L.’s
school fees.  The utility bills were registered in her name until August or
September of 2024.  But the evidence at trial also established that the mother
paid the mortgage on the home for 19 months, between January of 2019 and July
of 2020.

[
381
]

Although
he said that the mother would reimburse herself from the joint account, to
which he was the sole contributor, the father elsewhere said that he did not
have the funds to pay the 19 months, and that is why the mother paid.  This
begs the question as to how the mother reimbursed herself from a joint account
into which the father was the sole contributor, if he did not have the funds.

[
382
]

The
father was not the sole contributor into the joint account either, as he
claimed, even if the mother reimbursed herself.  Rather, the joint account was
maintained to receive the rental income earned on a jointly owned property, and
then to pay expenses.  This continued after the signing of the Separation
Agreement.

[
383
]

In
addition to the fact that the rental income was used to cover the carrying
costs for which the father was supposed to be responsible, the father did not
otherwise pay them all.  The evidence established that the mother sometimes covered
other items when there was a shortfall, in addition to the 19 months of
mortgage payments.  It has only been since July of 2024 that the father took
over managing the rental income and he started depositing it into his personal
account.

[
384
]

Notably,
the mother was also responsible for arranging and managing all of the tenants,
that resulted in the earned rental income.

(2)        The Father Abandoned Calling His Proposed Expert to
Testify

[
385
]

Regarding
the father’s second statement in his trial affidavit, that his expert opined
that the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement is a genuine document, the father
did not in the end call his expert to testify.  There were also shifting
positions and maneuvering regarding the expert evidence about the validity of
the Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement, although in this instance, it was caused
exclusively by the father.

[
386
]

The
Trial Scheduling Endorsement Form states that the father would be serving the
expert report of Sarba Sohail by September 30, 2024, and that he would seek to
qualify the witness in the area of “forensic assessment of cohabitation
agreement and signature of Applicant”.  The form states that the mother would

The Validity of the Separation Agreement on the Merits

,

D.

Findings
and Conclusions Regarding Whether the Parenting Terms in the Separation
Agreement Should Be Disregarded

[
416
]

Based
on the guidance in
Anderson v. Anderson
,
the applicable legislative
purposes to use as the “yardstick”, recognize that parental autonomy and
deference are important principles, subject to a child’s best interests, which must
remain paramount and at the forefront.  In other words, deference yields to
best interests, when there is a conflict:  see
C. (M.A.) v. K.(M.),
2009
ONCJ 18
at ¶
47-48
.

[
417
]

In
particular:

(a)

Regarding
deference,
section 2(10)
of the
Family Law Act

provides that a domestic
contract dealing with a matter that is also dealt with in this Act prevails
unless this Act provides otherwise; and

(b)

Similarly,
section 68 of the
Children’s Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990 c. C. 12
, as
amended,
reads that, “[w]here a domestic contract as defined in the
Family
Law Act

makes provision in respect of a matter that is provided for in this
Part, the contract prevails except as otherwise provided in Part IV of the
Family
Law Act”;
but

(c)

Section
56(1)
of the
Family Law Act
,
which is contained in Part IV,

provides
that “[i]n the determination of a matter respecting the education, moral
training or decision-making responsibility or parenting time with respect to a
child, the court may disregard any provision of a domestic contract pertaining
to the matter where, in the opinion of the court,
to do so is in the best
interests of the child
”; and

(d)

Section
19
(a) of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
,
provides as a purpose of Part
III, “to ensure that applications to courts respecting decision-making
responsibility, parenting time, contact and guardianship with respect to
children will be determined on the basis of the best interests of the
children.”

[
418
]

The
parenting terms of the Separation Agreement were never incorporated into a
final Order of this Court and this is not a variation proceeding.  A material
change test doesn’t apply:  see
B.C.J.B. v. E-R.R.R.,
2020 ONCJ 438
¶
82-90
.

The cumulative evidence that I have taken into account in deciding to disregard
the parenting terms under
section 56(1)
of the
Family Law Act
,
began
prior to the execution of the Separation Agreement.  I find the Court can
consider all of the evidence relevant to parenting in reaching this conclusion:
see
Molloy v. Molloy,
1991 CarswellOnt 3554
¶ 15
.

[
419
]

As
such, the allegation that the father put L. in the middle, by having her create
a parenting schedule, was proven.  So was the fact that the father also
overrode what the child had written as the parenting schedule.  The father
demonstrated very little insight during this trial about how he put the child
at the center of this, when he was testifying in chief about the conversations
he had with L. at the time the schedule was created.

[
420
]

But
I don’t really need to address the impact of this much further.  Even if there
is some material change type test that applies, or the evidence prior to the
Separation Agreement should not have been considered by me, it nevertheless
remains so that things have very much changed since the signing of the
Separation Agreement.    The evidence to that effect, was overwhelming.

[
421
]

The
Separation Agreement contains a severability clause.  My findings following
this trial about what new parenting arrangements are in the child’s best
interests do not result in the balance of the Separation Agreement falling by
the wayside.
For these reasons, it is not necessary to
have resort to the other arguments about duress, financial disclosure or legal
advice under
section 56(4)
of the
Family Law Act
,
to dispose of the
arguments about the validity of the Separation Agreement as it pertains to the parenting
terms.

[
422
]

In
conclusion, the parenting terms in the Separation Agreement shall be
disregarded under
section 56(1)
of the
Family Law Act
.

E.

Findings
and Conclusions Regarding Whether the Child Support Terms in the Separation
Agreement Should Be Disregarded

[
423
]

As
with the parenting terms, the parties did not need to mount a wholesale attack
of the Separation Agreement to seek child support terms at this trial that are
different from those contained in it, either.  The applicable legislative
purposes to use as the “yardstick” regarding the child support terms of the
Separation Agreement, once again recognize autonomy and deference are important
principles, but they also include the need to ensure that parents are providing
properly for the support of their children.

[
424
]

More
particularly:

(a)

Again
regarding deference,
section 2(10)
of the
Family Law Act

provides that a
“domestic contract dealing with a matter that is also dealt with in this Act
prevails unless this Act provides otherwise”; but

(b)

Section
56(1.1)
of the
Family Law Act

provides that “[i]n the determination of a
matter respecting the support of a child, the court may disregard any provision
of a domestic contract pertaining to the matter where the provision is
unreasonable having regard to the child support guidelines, as well as to any
other provision relating to support of the child in the contract”;

(c)

“The
preamble to the
Family Law Act

reads:  “[w]
hereas it is desirable to encourage and strengthen the role
of the family; and whereas for that purpose it is necessary to recognize the
equal position of spouses as individuals within marriage and to recognize
marriage as a form of partnership; and whereas in support of such recognition
it is necessary to provide in law for the orderly and equitable settlement of
the affairs of the spouses upon the breakdown of the partnership, and
to
provide for other mutual obligations in family relationships, including the
equitable sharing by parents of responsibility for their children
” [my
emphasis added];

(d)

Section
31(1)
of the
Family Law Act

contains the obligation of every parent to
provide support, to the extent he or she is capable of doing so, for his or her
minor child; and

(e)

The
four objectives of the
Guidelines
are to establish a fair standard of
support for children that ensures they benefit from the financial means of
their parents, to reduce conflict and tension between the parents, to improve
the efficiency of the legal process by giving guidance, and to ensure the
consistent treatment of parents and their children who are in similar
circumstances.

[
425
]

Having
regard to
section 56(1.1)
of the
Family law Act

and these other
statutory provisions, the child support provisions in the Separation Agreement
are no longer reasonable, as of January 28, 2025.  Since that date, the child
is no longer in a shared parenting arrangement.

[
426
]

The
situation prior to January 28, 2025 is different, for the reasons I summarized
