section 56(1.1)
.

F.

Findings
and Conclusions Regarding Whether the Property Terms in the Separation
Agreement Should Be Set Aside

[
427
]

That
leaves the property provisions and the releases, and the parties’ other
arguments about duress, disclosure and legal advice.  Neither side has
satisfied me that any of these grounds have been made out.

(1)       Duress

[
428
]

Section
56(4)
(c) of the
Family Law Act

provides that a court may, on
application, set aside a domestic contract or a provision in it, otherwise in
accordance with the law of contract.  At ¶ 53 of
Ludmer v. Ludmer,
2013 ONSC
784
,
Penny J. described duress as follows:

Duress involves a coercion of the will or a situation in
which one party has no realistic alternative but to submit to pressure.
There can be no duress without evidence of an attempt by one party to dominate
the will of the other at the time of the execution of the contract.  To
prove duress, the applicant must show that she was compelled to enter into the
marriage contract out of fear of actual or threatened harm of some kind.
There must be something more than stress associated with a potential breakdown
in familial relations.  There must be credible evidence demonstrating that
the complaining party was subject to intimidation or illegitimate pressure to
sign the agreement.

[
429
]

I
do not accept that the father was under some kind of undue pressure because of
the mother’s 2022 proceeding.  The case had only just begun when the mother
obtained the
ex parte
Order of Bruhn J.  The father could have attended before
this Court and sought to set the order aside.  He could have sought legal
advice, just as he said he did, before taking the child from her gymnastics.

[
430
]

Regarding
the mother, I appreciate what Chappel J. wrote at ¶ 352 and 353 of
Kinsella
v. Mills, 20209 ONSC 4785,
that the dynamics of the parties’ relationship
and of the interactions between them around the time the contract was signed
may be relevant to the analysis.  Evidence of a history of abuse or
intimidation may provide a critical backdrop to appreciating the undercurrents
that were at play when the contract was executed, and whether the aggrieved
party acted under coercion that fell within the realm of duress.  At the same
time, “vulnerability does not equate with duress”.

[
431
]

While
I do find that the parenting provisions in the Separation Agreement are not in
L.’s best interests, in part because of the findings made about family
violence, that is separate from making a finding of duress.  I do not accept
that mother was under pressure rising to the level of duress because the father
had overheld L. when the schedule was created.

[
432
]

The
mother herself had already obtained an Order in her favour when she signed the
Separation Agreement.  She could have taken further steps.  Regardless of
whether she spoke to Ms. Yehia about it or not
[14]
,
she had access to a lawyer whom she had retained around this time frame.

[
433
]

In
short, I find absolutely no merit to a claim by either of these parents, that
one or the other was under pressure or exploited because the overholding that
had happened, and based on some kind of fear of what might happen in Court.  The
fact that someone intends to litigate (or in this case, the fact that a proceeding
was already brought) is not duress:  see
Aghdasi v. Asiyaban,
2024 ONSC 3472

¶
238
.
Rather, the fact there was a pending case meant there was
actually a forum for both of these parties to bring forward their issues, a
forum which both parties would liberally access two years later, once this
round got underway.  Both parties’ competing arguments based on duress are
dismissed.

(2)       The Absence of Legal Advice

[
434
]

While
also relevant to duress, the complaints about the validity of the Separation
Agreement were separately framed to include specific arguments about the
absence of legal advice.

[
435
]

Section
56(4)
(b) of the
Family Law Act

provides that a court may, on
application, set aside a domestic contract or a provision in it, if a party did
not understand the nature or consequences of the domestic contract.  Section
56(4)(b) is broader than common law grounds for setting aside a contract, such
as
non est factum.
Unlike
non est factum,
section 56(4)(b) does
not make a party’s failure to exercise due diligence a bar to relief under the
clause:  see
Stewart v. Foreman,
2005 ONCJ 193
¶
21
.
However there is
no requirement in this provision, or otherwise, that a party must have
independent legal advice: see also
Anderson v. Anderson
¶
8
.

[
436
]

At
¶ 27 of
Duck v. Boshold,
2009 CanLii 65813
(S.C.J.)
,
Healey J.
summarized the law relating to the impact of a lack of independent legal advice,
including:

(a)

The
absence of independent legal advice does not automatically impugn the validity
of a domestic contract, but rather is a factor for the court to consider along
with all the other circumstances;

(b)

The
degree of professional assistance received by the parties will often overcome
any systemic imbalances between the parties, but this is always a question of
fact; and

(c)

Where
the spouse could have received independent legal advice but chose not to,
courts will be loath to set aside the agreement.

[
437
]

I
appreciate that the Separation Agreement says the parties had legal advice, and
both sides testified that they did not.  If true, they shouldn’t have put that
clause in their document.  But at the same time, as I have already said when
dealing with duress, they could have obtained legal advice.  And if they in
fact did not, they made a choice.

[
438
]

What
the parties both agreed to during this trial, is that they arranged to have a
notary witness their signatures on the Separation Agreement, because they
wanted it to have more legal formality or weight.  This is evidence that they
turned their minds to what they were doing.

[
439
]

The
property provisions were not complicated.  They address a single asset, the
equity of which was being divided:  see
Anderson v. Anderson
¶
5, 11, 83
.
As
I explain further next when addressing the complaints about non-disclosure, the
parties knew what they were bargaining for respecting the property provisions
in the Separation Agreement.  They turned their mind to how much equity was at
stake, and who would get what.

(3)        Lack
of Financial Disclosure

[
440
]

Section
56(4)(a) provides that a court may, on application, set aside a domestic
contract or a provision in it, if a party failed to disclose to the other significant
assets, or significant debts or other liabilities, existing when the domestic
contract was made.

[
441
]

While
I also appreciate that the Separation Agreement states that the parties made
complete, fair and accurate disclosure to each other on all financial matters
reflected in the Separation Agreement, and while I appreciate there are problems
with the father’s non-disclosure about his income for child support, the
complaint about non-disclosure relevant to the property terms of the Separation
Agreement is quite different.

[
442
]

At
¶ 47-48 of
Quinn v. Epstein Cole LLP,
2007 CanLii 45714
(S.C.J.)
,
Brown
J. wrote that a general awareness of the assets of the other party may be
sufficient to avoid setting aside an agreement.  Parties are expected to use
due diligence;  a person cannot fail to ask and then complain about inadequate
disclosure.  These paragraphs of the decision also set out that there is a two-stage
analysis under
section 56(4)
(a).   First, the party seeking to set aside the
agreement must demonstrate that the other failed to discharge his or her duty
to disclose significant assets (or liabilities).  What is required to establish
that, is further described in ¶ 47.  If the Court finds that there has been
such a failure, the Court must determine, on the facts of the case, whether to
exercise its discretion to rescind the domestic contract.  The burden of proof
lies on the party seeking to set the contract aside.  The discretion is
exercised according to a number of factors listed in the case.

[
443
]

I
am not even satisfied that a finding should be made that one or the other party
did not disclose, even if nothing was exchanged.  Assuming that I could or
should make a finding of significant non-disclosure here (which I do not), the
discretionary factors listed in
Quinn v. Epstein Cole LLP
do not
militate in favour of setting the Separation Agreement aside either. This is
not a case of the failure to ask and then provide, misrepresentation, or
concealment.

[
444
]

The
Thornhill Property was a joint asset.  They both knew they owned it.  They both
had the obligation to look into its value.  There was some evidence from the
father, that they did that.  Even if that was untrue;  the mother was a joint
owner;  she had a responsibility to look into it too.  The parties even
negotiated back and forth to come up with a purchase price.

[
445
]

Relatedly,
the father went on to argue in his trial affidavit, the mother received an
“improvident bargain”.  He said this because she received a $10,000.00 up front
payment, the Separation Agreement entitled her to a $50,000.00 “equalization
payment” (even though the parties were not married), and a $200,000.00 payout
for a property that he beneficially owned, and which was dealt with in the
earlier Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement.

[
446
]

Regarding
the $10,000.00 payment, this had nothing to do with the property. This was the
repayment to the mother, of other funds that the father owed her.  Regarding
the argument about the mother getting an equalization payment, the Separation
Agreement does not actually use those words.  Rather ¶ 11 of the Separation
Agreement provides for a partial payment of $200,000.00 for the transfer of the
mother’s interest in the Thornhill Property, with the balance of $50,000.00 to
be paid on a deferred basis.  Yet the $50,000.00 was characterized as an
equalization payment during this trial, for some reason.  And I have found the
Cohabitation and Mortgage Agreement was not a genuine document.

[
447
]

Were
I just to focus on the $250,000.00 buyout amount in analyzing whether there was
an improvident bargain, what I find to be quite incredible, is that no one
called any documentary and expert appraisal evidence as to what the equity in
the Thornhill Property was at the time of the Separation Agreement, to
demonstrate exactly how off-side the property terms allegedly were.  All the
father did in his trial affidavit (and orally during the trial) was try to
embark upon some sort of calculation of his own to this effect.  It involved
backing out the renovation costs, which were not broken out and documented, and
which he may not have been entitled to back out anyway.

G.

Conclusions
Regarding the Validity of the Separation Agreement

[
448
]

The
requests to set the property provisions of the Separation Agreement aside on
their merits, are dismissed.

H.

The
Competing Motions to Amend Pleadings

[
449
]

Despite
that finding, the requests to amend pleadings are still on the table, because one
or even both of the parties seem to want to make trust claims, even if the

[
450
]

Rule
11(3) provides that on motion, the court shall give permission to a party to
amend an application, answer or reply, unless the amendment would disadvantage
another party in a way for which costs or an adjournment could not compensate.
As I wrote at ¶  304 -323 of
Lerus v. Vilgrain,
2020 ONCJ 77
:

(a)

A
request to amend a pleading will usually be granted.  The request is mandatory,
unless one of the exceptions applies;

(b)

Pleadings
may be amended up to, and even during a trial itself;

(c)

Family
litigation is different from civil litigation; and

(d)

There
should be flexibility when it comes to considering requests to amend.

[
451
]

But
were I to allow these mid-trial amendments, I would be doing so to allow the
parties to pursue claims that are barred by the releases in the Separation

see
McKay v. Vlazny,
2022 ONSC 1056
¶
7
;
see also
Moghimi v. Dashti,

2016 ONSC 2116
¶
19-21
.
And it bears repeating, that in the father’s
case, he wants to amend, after first trying to persuade the Court to enforce

[
452
]

The
father’s Notice of Motion dated June 17, 2025, his 14B Motion dated July 3,

The Property Provisions in the Separation Agreement Shall

]

parties are to implement the property terms of the Separation Agreement.  If

The Mother’s Claims for Post-Separation Adjustments and
Occupation Rent

[
454
]

The
mother has claims for post-separation adjustments of $47,319.23 (relating to

[
455
]

In
any event, the mother’s other claims for a post-separation accounting and

(a)

The mother
sold her interest in the property to the father in 2022;  and

(b)

The releases
in the Separation Agreement, particularly paragraph 21, are dispositive of those

[
456
]

The
real issue, is that the mother hasn’t been paid for her interest in the

K.

Prejudgment
Interest

[
457
]

The
mother has made a claim for prejudgment interest in her Application issued on
January 13, 2024.

[
458
]

Section
128(1)
of the
Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C. 43
, as amended,
provides
that a person who is entitled to an order for the payment of money is entitled
to claim and have included in the order an award of interest thereon at the
prejudgment interest rate, calculated from the date of the cause of action
arose to the date of the order.

[
459
]

Section
130(1)
of the
Courts of Justice Act

provides that the court may, where
it considers it just to do so in respect of the whole or any part of the amount
on which interest is payable under section 128, disallow interest, order
interest at a higher or lower rate, or allow interest for a period other than
provided in section 128.  Section 130(2) lists a number of factors that drive
the exercise of the Court’s discretion under section 130(1):  see also
R.L.
v. M.F.,
2025 ONCA 595
¶
81-90

[
460
]

No
one argued any of the exceptions in section 130(2).  Nonetheless, and out of an
abundance of caution only, having regard to sections 130(2)(b), (e) and (f) in
particular, I note the following:

(a)

On the
one hand, the mother testified that she did not enforce the Separation
Agreement because her priority was on L.  She also said she felt badly for the
father, because he was facing the loss of his professional license.  Whatever
her reasons, she delayed in taking any steps to enforce the outstanding
payments owing to her under the Separation Agreement;

(b)

On the
other hand, father clearly breached the property provisions.  Had the father
just complied with the property terms in the Separation Agreement, there would
have been no need for the mother to engage in any kind of deliberations about
whether to take enforcement steps, or not;

(c)

Furthermore,
had the father just complied with the terms, this onslaught of litigation about
what to do with the property terms in the Separation Agreement and the other claims,
may very well have been avoided;

(d)

The
mother told the father that she wanted to be removed from the mortgage at the time
of the mortgage renewal incident in November of 2023.  She then capitulated,
and agreed to renew.  The father benefitted from this;

(e)

The
father benefitted from the mother not taking other steps to enforce, for
example because she continued to manage the rental income for his benefit.
Notably now that she is not doing this anymore, there is no further tenant in
the basement as of the departure of the most recent tenant in March 2025; and

(f)

I
have denied the mother’s claim for a post-separation accounting.   While the
Separation Agreement does not give her an ongoing entitlement to share in the
rental income, what it notably does do though, is provide that she should be paid
a fee for booking (i.e. associated with her ongoing management of the rentals).
I would have considered ordering such a payment, had evidence been called about
it and had the fee been quantified, but this wasn’t done.  So I will just take that
contractual entitlement into account, not to quantify and order it, but for the
fact that the mother will not recover on it, when deciding why I find it fair
and just not to deny her presumptive entitlement to prejudgment interest.

[
461
]

Therefore,
there shall be an order for prejudgment interest in accordance with the statute
at the applicable rate.

[
462
]

No
one gave me a prejudgment interest calculation.  The prejudgment interest rate
for the first quarter of 2024 (when the mother’s Application was issued) was
5.3%. Two different calculations are required, as the parties agreed in the
Separation Agreement, that the father would purchase the mother’s interest in
the Thornhill Property by way of two payments made at different points in
time.

[
463
]

First,
the sum of $200,000.00 was due on signing the Separation Agreement.  My
calculation of prejudgment interest on this amount is therefore $37,317.81,
calculated as follows:

$200,000 x
5.3% / 365 days per year x 1285 days (i.e. the number of days between the
signing of the Separation Agreement on March 18, 2022 and the date of this
Judgment) = $37,317.81.

[
464
]

Second,
the further sum of $50,000.00 was due on November 24, 2023.  My calculation of
prejudgment interest on this amount is $4,857.12, calculated as follows:

$50,000 x
5.3% / 365 days per year x 669 days (i.e. this is the number of days between
November 24, 2023 and the date of this Judgment) =  $4,857.12.

[
465
]

Therefore,
the total amount of prejudgment interest owing, is
$42,174.93.

[
466
]

If
either side is of the view that I made a mathematical error only, they may
address that when costs are dealt with.  To be clear, this is not an
opportunity to argue about the Court’s decision to order prejudgment interest;
just to address mathematical errors, if either counsel sees one.

L.

Security
for Costs

[
467
]

Counsel
for the mother asked the Court to make an order for security for costs.  What

[

]

Having
regard to rule 24(13) of the
Family Law Rules,
I was told that there is

PART VIII:   PARENTING

A.        Applicable
Statutory Provisions

[
469
]

A
parenting order is defined in
section 18(1)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act

as an order made under
section 28
respecting decision-making responsibility
or parenting time with respect to a child.

[
470
]

Decision-making
responsibility is defined in
section 18(1)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act

as
the responsibility for making significant decisions about a child’s wellbeing,
including with respect to health, education, culture, language, religion and
spirituality, and significant extra-curricular activities.   Parenting time
means the time that a child spends in the care of a parent of the child,
whether or not the child is physically present with the parent during that
time.

[
471
]

Pursuant
to
section 28
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
, the Court may grant
decision-making responsibility or parenting time to one or more parents of the
child, it may determine any aspect of the incidents of the right to
decision-making responsibility or parenting time, and it may make any
additional order the Court considers necessary and proper in the circumstances,
including a non-exhaustive list of  seven kinds of orders.

[
472
]

The
Court’s only focus is on the best interests of the child when making a
parenting Order:  see
section 24(1)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
.  Pursuant
to section 24(2), the Court is to consider all factors related to the
circumstances of the child when determining best interests.  In so doing, it
must give primary consideration to the child’s physical, emotional and
psychological safety, security and well-being.

[
473
]

Section
24(3)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act

provides a non-exhaustive list of
ten factors that are related to a child’s circumstances, that help guide the
analysis.
No one legislative factor in section
24(3) has greater weight than the other, although there may be more evidence
about one factor versus another:
see
Libbus v.
Libbus
(2008)
,
2008 CanLII 53970 (ON SC)
,
62
R.F.L. (6
th
) 416 (Ont. S.C.J.)
¶88;
see also
Van de Perre v. Edwards, 201 SCC 60
¶
10
.

[
474
]

Pursuant
to
section 24(5)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
, the Court is not to
take into consideration the past conduct of any person unless the conduct is
relevant to the exercise of the person’s decision-making responsibility or
parenting time.  But in this case, there have been a multitude of allegations
about past parental behaviour, which I do find to be relevant to the exercise
of decision-making responsibility and parenting time.

B.        Applicable
Legal Principles and Analysis Concerning Joint Decision-Making Responsibility

[
475
]

There
are competing plans before the Court about which parent should be empowered to
make significant decisions about the child.  Theoretically, one of the remedial
options before the Court, would be to allocate some of all of that significant
decision-making jointly, or to divide it between the parents in some kind of
parallel parenting Order.
The legal principles applicable
to joint decision-making are well known:
see
Kaplanis v. Kaplanis,
2005 CanLII 1625
(Ont. C.A.)
:  see also
Roloson v. Clyde,
2017 ONSC 3642
¶
59
in which
Chappel J. provides a helpful list of factors to consider.

[
476
]

In
particular, it is well-known that joint decision-making is generally only
appropriate in cases where there is evidence of historical and appropriate
communication between the parents.   Just because one parent
professes an inability to communicate does not preclude an order joint
decision-making.  Nor is the standard of perfection required.  But where there
is poor communication, joint decision-making should not be ordered in the hopes
that two parents’ communication will improve.  There must be some evidence
before the Court that, despite their differences, the parents are able to communicate
effectively with one another.

C.        Analysis,
Findings and Conclusions Regarding L.’s Best Interests

(1)        The Nature and Strength of the Child’s Relationships
With Each Parent, Siblings, Grandparents and Others Who Play an Important Role
in the Child’s Life

[
477
]

Section
24(3)
(b) of the
Children’s Law Reform Act

lists as a factor related to
the child’s circumstances in the best interests’ analysis, the nature and
strength of the child’s relationships with each parent, siblings, grandparents
and any other person who plays an important role in the child’s life.

[
478
]

The
mother testified that she has a very good relationship with both of her
children.  She said they love and trust her.  I also heard that L. and her
sister V. have a close relationship, although V. has been involved in the
conflict with the father.  I heard some evidence about L. acting out in the
mother’s household.  The mother testified this happened after contact with the
father, or as a result of the conflict and pressure to which she has been
exposed.  This position is reasonable.

[
479
]

By
all accounts, L. and her father love each other.  But a consistent theme in
their relationship concerns the father’s behaviour and anger, and how that
impacts her.

[
480
]

L.
used to have a relationship with members of the father’s extended family.  But the
paternal grandmother and aunt have been drawn into the conflict at the behest
of the father.  The father’s sister is involved in two other court matters
regarding the mother and V., without much insight into its impact on L.

(2)        The Child’s Needs and the Parents’ Abilities and
Willingness to Meet Those Needs

[
481
]

Section
24(3)
(a) of the
Children’s Law Reform Act

includes as a factor related
to L.’s circumstances in a best interests’ analysis, her needs, given her age
and stage of development, such as her need for stability.  Section 24(3)(h)
lists as a factor for the analysis a consideration of the ability and
willingness of each person in respect of whom the order would apply to care for
and meet the needs of the child.

[
482
]

In
order to analyze these provisions properly, it is first necessary to articulate
what L.’s needs are.

[
483
]

L.
is a newly teenaged girl, who is driven, and who succeeds at school and in her
extra-curricular activities.  This needs to be supported and encouraged.  While
she has a desire and a need to have and maintain a healthy relationship with

and her father’s angry outbursts and instability.  Many court appearances ago,

challenge in this case, is how to achieve this.

(3)        The Parties’ Parenting of L.

[
484
]

In
addition to the parties’ parenting being relevant to their abilities and
willingness to meet L.’s needs,
section 24(3)
(d) lists as a factor related to
L.’s circumstances, the history of her care.  Despite the fact that the
Separation Agreement provided for shared parenting and L. has had a shared
schedule between no later than June of 2022, and January of 2025, I find that
the mother has been L.’s primary parent throughout.

[
485
]

The
mother testified that she has always been L.’s primary parent.  She testified
that she took responsibility for cooking and cleaning for L., arranging her
medical and dental appointments, bath time and home work.  In her
cross-examination, the mother clarified she did the majority of the child’s
home work with her, defining the division as the mother doing between 80 to
90%.  By contrast, the mother testified that the father was the “fun dad” when
the parties were together.

[
486
]

A
careful review of the evidence confirms this history of the mother being the
primary parent.

[
487
]

By
all accounts, L. and her father share a common interest in sports, including
basketball and football.  The father testified that he prioritizes basketball,
because of L.’s passion for it, and he sourced a school that would nurture her
athletic dreams.  However, on his own admission, during his examination-in-chief,
the father agreed that he had mostly been the “fun dad” and the mother was the

[
488
]

The
father testified that he is serious when it comes to L.’s education, though.  While
I accept that the father has an interest in L.’s education, I also accept the
mother’s evidence that she was the one who then did the “administrative” work
associated with implementing it, such as completing the forms, making the
payments for the school and liaising with teachers.  And as I explain below,
there was a recent mid-trial written exchange between the parties, where the

[
489
]

The
father did not know the name of L.’s current doctor (after the previous doctor
closed his office “a year or two ago”).  He hadn’t met all of L.’s teachers in
her current school.

(4)       Family Violence

[
490
]

While
it is now defined in
section 18(1)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
,
family
violence has always been relevant in the assessment of a child’s best
interests.  The statutory definition is broad. It means any conduct by a family
member towards another family member that is violent or threatening, that
constitutes a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour or that causes the
other family member to fear for their own safety or for that of another person,
and, in the case of a child, includes direct or indirect exposure to such
conduct.  A “family member” includes a member of a household of a child or of a
parent, as well as a dating partner of a parent who participates in the
activities of the household.

[
491
]

Section
18(2)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act

provides that conduct need not
constitute a criminal offence to amount to family violence, and family violence
includes a non-exhaustive list of acts, specifically physical abuse, threats,
harassment, and psychological abuse, among others.  The Court is not precluded
from finding that other conduct fits within its meaning, too:  see ¶ 27 of
McLellan
v. Birbilis,
2021 ONSC 7084
.

[
492
]

At
¶ 143 of
Barendgret v. Grebliunas,
2022 SCC 22
,
Karatkatsanis J. wrote
,

“[t]he suggestion that domestic abuse or family violence has no impact on
the children and has nothing to do with the perpetrator’s parenting ability is
untenable.  Research indicates that children who are exposed to family violence
are at risk of emotional and behavioural problems throughout their lives…. Harm
can result from direct or indirect exposure to domestic conflicts, for example
by observing the incident, experiencing its aftermath, or hearing about it”.
At ¶ 144, she wrote that allegations of family violence are “notoriously
difficult to prove”.  Proof of even one incident may raise safety concerns for
the victim or may overlap with and enhance the significance of other factors,
such as the need for limited contact or support.

[
493
]

At
¶ 146 of
Barendgret v. Grebliunas,
Karatkatsanis J. described the
statutory provisions about family violence as a “critical consideration in the
best interests analysis”.  While she was writing about the mirror provisions in
the
Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2
nd
Supp.), as amended
in
the context of a relocation case
,
their critical importance applies
equally under the
Children’s Law Reform Act
,
in all parenting cases, not
just relocation ones.

[
494
]

Section
24(3)
(j) of the
Children’s Law Reform Act

provides that family violence
and its impact on, among other things, the ability and willingness of any
person who engaged in the family violence to care for and meet the needs of the
child, and the appropriateness of making an order that would require persons to
cooperate on issues affecting the child, are factors related to the child’s
circumstances in the best interests’ analysis.

[
495
]

The
father denied that he ever engaged in either verbal or physical family
violence.  I have already made specific findings earlier in this Judgment, to
the contrary.  Because of their central importance to this case, I intend to
list and summarize them again here.  In summary:

(a)

The
father had a physical altercation with V. on Family Day in 2018.  This incident
occurred when L. was in the home.  L. was just 5 at the time;

(b)

The
father physically assaulted the mother by pulling her hair and causing her
physical pain.  L. was no older than 6 years old at the time, and was present
in the home when this occurred;

(c)

The
father destroyed L.’s bedroom for the first time in a fit of rage in January of
2020;

(d)

The
father destroyed the child’s bedroom for the second time and destroyed the
mother’s work laptop computer on April 3, 2020.  The father assaulted the mother
by throwing anti-bacterial gel.  The child, who was present in the home when
this occurred, was 7 years old;

(e)

The
father damaged the wall in L.’s bedroom in December of 2021, because he was
frustrated during the child’s morning routine.  This incident occurred in the
child’s presence, who was then 9 years old;

(f)

The
father choked and smothered the mother in July of 2022.  This incident occurred
in the presence of the child, then still 9 years old.  She uttered that the
father was going to kill her mother; and

(g)

The
father has made numerous crude statements about the mother’s sexuality.  He has
also abused her in writing, as explained earlier with reference to the Columbia
Trip in 2020, and the Disney Trip in 2024.

[
496
]

An
additional challenge with the father’s denial that he ever engaged in verbal
abuse of the mother in particular, is that the father engaged in verbal abuse
of the mother, under oath, right under the watch of this Court.  When the
father was asked point blank about acts of physical violence, he was abusive

(5)        The Parents’ Mental Health

[

Both

2024 ONSC 2368
,
Kraft J. referred to the Revised AFCC-Ontario
Parenting Guide, Microsoft Word – AFCC-O Parenting Plan Guide (Version 2.0,
December 2021).doc (afccontario.ca) and the principles discussed therein
regarding mental illness as instructive.  At ¶ 106 of
Gerasimoloulos v.
Sambirsky
,
Kraft J. excerpted from page 48 of the guide as follows:

Parental
Substance Abuse or Mental Illness

Mental illness
or substance abuse problems may adversely affect parenting if that parent is
emotionally unavailable, is unable to adequately discipline and set limits, or
provide a safe environment for the children. In such cases, it may be necessary
to consider alternative parenting arrangements such as therapeutic
intervention, supervised parenting time, or limited parenting time until the
concerns have been satisfactorily addressed.
Protocols may need to be
put in place for ongoing or periodic monitoring and for a resumption or gradual
increase in parenting time
.

To the extent
that parents with a mental illness or substance abuse issue are compliant with
their treatment plan, or parenting is not affected, regular parenting time can
be established or resumed. In many cases, it will be beneficial to
proactively plan for a relapse, with provisions to address the affected
parent’s responsibility to communicate the relapse and the arrangements that
will be in place to ensure the children’s safety (e.g., supervisory
arrangements, switch to virtual parenting time, temporary suspension of
contact) while the parent takes steps to address their situation. Parents
should also consider whether their children may benefit from psycho-educational
programs to assist them in understanding the issue their parent is
experiencing; in many situations, this may be an important element of safety
planning.

Unless a
parent with mental illness or substance abuse issues acknowledges their
condition and its effect on parenting, it may be necessary for the courts to be
involved in making a parenting plan. It should, however, also be appreciated
that even if a parent has substance abuse or mental health issues, if those are
properly addressed, in the long-term children will often want and benefit from
a relationship with that parent.

didn’t you see me’ and he won’t understand and there will just be too much

therapy would help.

[
550
]

Ms. de Munnik testified that at the June 19, 2025 mid-trial
interview, L.’s views were consistent with these prior, post-Christmas incident

supervised.  This meeting occurred before the damaging session with Ms. Geraldo,
on July 9, 2025.

[
551
]

Ms. de Munnik offered a number of reasons as to why she was of the
view, that L.’s views were independent.

[
552
]

I acknowledge that L.’s views changed after the Christmas incident,
in that she was willing to see her father unsupervised before, and she was
unwilling after.  But that focuses on the wrong thing.  That is not really what

[
553
]

What I find changed, was L.’s confidence and willingness to speak

D.        Conclusions About the Remedy Respecting the Parenting
Issues

[
554
]

Although both parties provided draft Orders at the outset
of the trial, and different draft Orders for closing submissions, the entire
range of remedial options regarding parenting were on the table during this
trial.  The Court is
not bound
by either
side’s positions, where it is of the view that they are not consistent with the
children’s best interests:  see
A.M. v. C.H.,
2019 ONCA 764
¶
29
;
see also
Richardson v. Richardson,
2019 ONCA 983
¶
25-31
.
T
he Court is not adopting either side’s draft Orders
tendered at the end of the trial in their entirety.

(1)        Conclusions Respecting Decision-Making
Responsibility

[
555
]

I find that any form of joint decision-making is
contraindicated for this family.

[
556
]

I am mindful that courts sometimes order some form of joint
decision-making, even in the face of parental conflict, where such an order is
considered necessary to preserve the balance of power between the parents.
This is particularly in cases where both parties are caring and competent
parents, but where one party has been primarily responsible for the conflict.

But I do not find this to be applicable here.  The father needs to have a
serious look at his own conduct, and his own role in the fracturing of his
relationship with L.  The Court is concerned that any form of joint
decision-making is more likely to inflame the parents’ conflict and expose L.
to it.  That very much militates against such an Order:  see
S.S. v. S.
K.
,

2013 ONCJ 432
¶
43
.

[
557
]

Sometimes where a court empowers one parent to make significant
decisions for a child, it will impose on that parent a duty to consult before
deciding.  Because of the great concern I have about L. being exposed to any
more conflict, the father continuing to abuse the mother, and how that might
impact her parenting, I would not even impose that.  The duty being imposed
will be to inform briefly in writing, but not to consult.

[
558
]

In
the result, the Court finds it must choose between one of the parents.
The Court selects the mother.

(2)        Conclusions Respecting
Parenting Time

[
559
]

P
ursuant to
section 24(6)
of the
Children’s
Law Reform Act
, in allocating parenting time, the Court shall give effect
to the principle that a child should have as much time with each spouse as is
consistent with the best interests of the child.   How this provision is to be
interpreted, was also recently addressed by the Supreme Court in
Barendregt
v. Grebliunas

at
¶
133-135
.
As Karatkatsanis J. wrote, there is no
presumption of shared parenting arrangements, equal parenting time or even
regular parenting time.  The principle in section 24(6) is “only significant to
the extent that is in the child’s best interests;  it must not be used to
detract from this inquiry”.

[
560
]

The father’s principal positions, that there should be some
form of a shared parenting arrangement, or even a “blackout period” with the child
in his primary care, were unrealistic and not tied to the evidence.  The latter
depended on a finding of alienation, that the Court has not made.

[
561
]

That
leaves the mother’s and the OCL’s positions that there be supervision (which
the Court can order under
section 34
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
),
or something else, and the father’s alternative position that if there is to be
supervision, it should be supervised by his mother or sister.

[
562
]

Based
on this record I seriously considered the complete termination of the father’s
parenting time, notwithstanding the child’s views and preferences, that she
wants to still have some form of contact with him.   At ¶ 138-140 of
V.S.J.
v. L.J.G.,
2004 CanLii 17126
, Blishen J. wrote, citing
M.
(B.P.) v. M. (B.L.D.E.)
(1991),
1992 CanLII 8642 (ON CA)
,
42 R.F.L. (3d) 349 (Ont.C.A.)
,
that
supervised parenting time is seldom viewed as an indefinite order or a long
term solution.
At ¶ 135-137,  drawing from other cases, Blishen
J. provided a list of factors to consider when a Court is faced with the
difficult decision about whether to terminate parenting time altogether.
The factors that she listed are also relevant to whether to order supervised
parenting time.  Multiple factors are generally existent in the cases.

[
563
]

The
factors that Blishen J. listed are:

(a)

long term harassment and harmful behaviours towards the custodial
parent causing that parent and the child stress and or fear;

(b)

a history of violence; unpredictable,
uncontrollable behaviour; alcohol, drug abuse which has been witnessed by the
child and/or presents a risk to the child’s safety and well being;

(c)

extreme parental alienation which has resulted in changes of
custody and, at times, orders for no parenting time to the former custodial
parent;

(d)

ongoing severe denigration of the other parent;

(e)

lack of relationship or attachment between noncustodial parent
and child;

(f)

neglect or abuse to a child on visits; and

(g)

older children’s wishes and preferences to terminate
parenting time.

[
564
]

A number of
these features are present here.

[
565
]

Blishen J. further
wrote that where there had been an attempt at supervision that has proven
unworkable, a termination must be considered.  And if there is an unwillingness
on the part of a parent to deal with the underlying issues necessitating
supervision, then supervision may not be a viable option.   These features are
present here.

[
566
]

When
considering what remedy to Order, I recognize that I heard Ms. Geraldo’s
views.  To be clear, I am not adopting any of Ms. Geraldo’s revised recommendations,
just because Ms. Geraldo gave them as a professional witness.  The Court was
able to form its own impressions.  And one difficulty I have with Ms. Geraldo’s
particular recommendation for supervised parenting time, while the father is in
a separate stream addresses his mental health, is that I have no confidence
that the father will not engage in repeat behaviour in a supervised setting
with a different person supervising at the helm in the mean time.  Although the
July 9 session was a therapy session, it was also in effect a form of
supervised contact, and it ended in a disaster.  As Ms. Geraldo candidly
admitted when she apologized to the child, she had lost control.

[
567
]

I
do not fault Ms. Geraldo.  The father was ungovernable in his interactions with
the mother and the child at times, in his dealings with the OCL, in his
dealings with the Society at times, and repeatedly in Court, too.  In
L.S.
v. M.A.F.,
2021 ONCJ 554
,
Sherr J. had before him a father who:

… presented as
a very angry person during the hearing.  He reacted to routine questioning from
the mother’s counsel with hostility, defiance and at times, sarcasm.  His anger
quickly escalated and was out of proportion.  He tried to control the narrative
during questioning and became frustrated when he could not do this.  He didn’t
listen.  He misunderstood questions and was very suspicious.  He was
confrontational and argumentative.  He was particularly infuriated about the
mother’s child support claim.

[
568
]

Sherr
J.’s description of the father’s trial conduct in that case is a strikingly apt
descriptor of how the father behaved during this trial before me.

[
569
]

I
am concerned about a professional supervisor’s ability to handle the father and
to insulate the child from his conduct. Certainly therefore, the father’s
request that either his mother or sister supervise is a non-starter for the
exact same reason.  Furthermore, the paternal grandmother did not testify.  His
sister was not asked if she understood what her roles and responsibilities as a
supervisor would be.  And for instance, one of the things that the child needs
to be insulated from, is further discussion about the Christmas incident.  Yet
the father’s sister has a video.  Both she and the father are invested in
disclosing their “truth” about what happened.

[
570
]

On the other hand, despite the
admonition that supervision is not usually a long-term solution, Blishen J.
also recognized that there may be occasions, where medium or longer-term
supervised parenting time will be in a child’s best interests, and it should be
considered as an alternative to a complete termination.  That may be the case
here, where the child (now age 13) wishes to continue to have contact with her
father, which the Court is trying to
very much give effect to.  But
for the consistency of those expressed views, the outcome would have been a
termination.

[
571
]

So
to give effect to the child’s desire to maintain a relationship with the
father, I will adopt the OCL’s closing submission about the form of
supervision.  I find it to be the only way to balance the problems that have
presented here, short of a termination.  For these reasons I intend only to
order short, supervised visits, by a professional supervisor, to occur
virtually.  If the father misbehaves, any individual virtual visit can be
terminated with the click of a button by either the child, or the supervisor.  And
if the problems continue and become too overwhelming to manage, then the visits
may very well be ended by default (such as if the child refuses to reattend, or
if the supervisor becomes unwilling to offer the service).  I would not view
the termination of supervised visits arising out of any misconduct of the
father during those visits, as a material change warranting a further
proceeding, for a different parenting arrangement.

(3)        Conclusions Respecting Additional Terms and Conditions

[
572
]

I
considered ordering the father to take a number of steps to address his
behaviour and mental health after which there could be a review.  But I have

[
573
]

Similarly,
I considered ordering that the father take a number of steps before the

[

One
of the terms will be that the father undergo a mental health assessment.  The

]

The
Court has no other option than to adopt Mr. Sheena’s submissions in response to

[
577
]

There
will be a leave requirement before the father can launch another round of
litigation.  Leave will be considered on an
ex parte
basis.  The mother
does not need to engage with the father or the Court, at the leave stage.   I
find this is a further safeguard to protect this child from exposure to another

[
578
]

Finally,
I was not asked to grant a restraining Order under
section 35
of the
Children’s
Law Reform Act
.
I would have considered such a request, had I been. The

section 28(1)
(c) of the
Children’s Law Reform Act.
I intend to do so in
L.’s best interests, to give effect to the terms of this Order, and in light of

[
579
]

So
that it is clear, this implicates the mother, too.  She has to follow these

PART IX:      CHILD SUPPORT

A. Applicable
Statutory Provisions

[
580
]

The
obligation of a parent to provide support for his or her child is provided for
in
section 31(1)
of the
Family Law Act
.
Section 33
makes provision for
child support applications to be brought under provincial legislation for
unmarried parents
.
Pursuant to section 34(1)(f), the Court may make an
order for child support for periods before the date of the Order
.

[
581
]

Section
33(11) directs that when the Court makes a child support Order, it shall do in
accordance with the
Guidelines
.
One question that I find arises on this
record though, particularly when considering the competing retroactive claims, is
whether the $500.00 monthly amount of child support in the Separation Agreement
even departed from the
Guidelines
in the past
.
I am by not
certain that it did.  Insofar as prospective support (as of February 1, 2025)
is concerned, I would rely on
section 56(1.1)
of the
Family Law Act
.

B.        Retroactivity

[
582
]

Just
because the Court has the power to make a retroactive Order, doesn’t mean that
it should, at least not for the entire period in issue in this case.

[
583
]

At
¶ 113 and 114 of
Colucci v. Colucci,
2021 SCC 24
,
Martin J. summarized
the principles that apply to cases in which there are claims under the
Divorce
Act

both to retroactively increase or to decrease child support.  Although
Colucci
v. Colucci

involved the variation of an existing Order under the
Divorce
Act,
and this case does not, a number of the principles set out in those
paragraphs of
Colucci v. Colucci

are nevertheless instructive.

[
584
]

In
particular, regarding the mother’s request for retroactive support prior to the
Separation Agreement, and to retroactively increase the amount of child support
in the Separation Agreement thereafter:

(a)

There
is a presumption of retroactively increasing child support to the date the
recipient gave the payor effective notice, up to three years before formal
notice of the application to vary.  Because of informational asymmetry,
effective notice requires only that the recipient broached the subject of an
increase with the payor;

(b)

Where
no effective notice is given by the recipient parent, child support should
generally be increased back to the date of formal notice;

(c)

There
is discretion to depart from the presumptive date of retroactivity where the
result would be unfair.  The factors in
D.B.S. v. S.R.G.,
2006 SCC 37
,
as
applied in
Michel v. Graydon,
2020 SCC 24
continue to guide this
exercise of discretion.  If the payor failed to disclose a material increase in
income, that failure qualifies as blameworthy conduct and the date of
retroactivity will generally be the date of the increase in income; and

(d)

Once
the court has determined that support should be retroactively increased to a
particular date, the increase must be quantified.  The proper amount of support
for each year since the date of retroactivity must be calculated in accordance
with the
Guidelines
.

[
585
]

Regarding
the father’s request to retroactively decrease the child support set out in the
Separation Agreement and for an overpayment (if that is still being pursued):

(a)

There
is a presumption in favour of retroactively decreasing child support to the
date the payor gave effective notice, up to three years before formal notice of
the application to vary.  In the decrease context, effective notice requires
clear communication of the change in circumstances accompanied by the disclosure
of any available documentation necessary to substantiate the change and allow
the recipient parent to meaningfully assess the situation;

(b)

Where
no effective notice is given by the payor parent, child support should
generally be varied back to the date of formal notice, or to a later date where
the payor has delayed making complete disclosure in the course of the
proceeding;

(c)

The
Court retains discretion to depart from the presumptive date of retroactivity
where the result would be unfair.  The
D.B.S.

factors (adapted to the
decrease context) guide the exercise of discretion.  The factors are whether
the payor had an understandable reason for the delay in seeking a decrease, the
payor’s conduct, the child’s circumstances, and hardship to the payor if
support is not decreased (viewed in context of hardship to the child and
recipient if support is decreased).  The payor’s efforts to pay what they can
and to communicate and disclose income information on an ongoing basis will
often be a key consideration under the factor of payor conduct; and

(d)

Once
the court has determined that support should be retroactively decreased to a
particular date, the decrease must be quantified.  The proper amount of support
for each year since the date of retroactivity must be calculated in accordance
with the
Guidelines
.

C.        Findings and Conclusions Regarding the Mother’s Claim for

]

The
mother’s claim for retroactive child support between the date of separation

The

The

unemployed, or at least he did not receive a pay cheque, from January of 2023
to March of 2024.  Finally, in his trial affidavit, the father said he has a
debt of $400,000.00 related to the original business purchase.  If that is the
case, this is not readily apparent on any of his family law financial
statements, below.  He said that there are two active lawsuits against him with
potential liabilities totaling $3.1 million also.  He said he anticipates a
possible settlement of around $1 million per lawsuit.  One of his family financial
statements, below, places this potential liability at $3.1 million, not $2
million as the trial affidavit indicates.   Supporting documentation for these
alleged liabilities, was not tendered either.

(3)        The Father’s Current Self-Employment as the Owner of a
Marijuana Business

[
607
]

Following
the father’s suspension, he purchased a marijuana store.  But the father’s
position is that he is not the owner of the marijuana business though; his
sister is the owner.  In short, while he testified that he initially planned to
buy the business on his own, things changed.  The second plan was that his
sister was going to “partner” with him.  Then, he decided he didn’t want to be
the “main” person, and so his sister bought the business, not him.

(4)        Findings and Conclusions About the Ownership of the
Marijuana Business

[
608
]

Although
the Ontario Court of Appeal’s comments were made in the context of a tort
claim, at ¶45 of
Leitch v. Novak,
2020 ONCA 257
,
Hourigan J.A. wrote:

There is a related malady that often works hand-in-hand
with nondisclosure to deny justice in family law proceedings. The problem is
what I will call "invisible litigants". These are family members or
friends of a family law litigant who insert themselves into the litigation
process. They go beyond providing emotional support during a difficult time to
become active participants in the litigation. Usually, their intentions are
good, and their interference makes no difference in the ultimate result.
However, sometimes they introduce or reinforce a win-at-all-costs litigation
mentality. These invisible litigants are willing to break both the spirit and
letter of the family law legislation to achieve their desired result, including
by facilitating the deliberate hiding of assets or income.

[
609
]

I
find this to be the situation here;  the father’s sister is an “invisible
litigant”.  I agree with the mother’s position.  I do not accept, as the father
argued, that his sister is the owner of the marijuana store.  I find the father
is the true owner.  I find the father and his sister attempted to present a
different state of affairs in an attempt to deceive the Court and conceal the true
extent of an income source that he has available to pay child support.  I make
these findings for the following several reasons.

[
610
]

First
of all, during her examination-in-chief, the mother testified that the father
is the true owner of the marijuana business because:

(a)

the father had spoken to her about the marijuana business in 2022 and
2023;

(b)

she observed phone calls occurring between the father and a broker;

(c)

she helped him find the marijuana store;

(d)

she talked with him about the changes he wanted to make to the business;
and

(e)

she helped him with some of the set up of the business.

[
611
]

Quite
apart from what the mother said about it, the father’s and his sister’s
explanations were incredible.  In particular:

(a)

In her
trial affidavit, the father’s sister said she was on disability leave from her
job in 2022 and the idea of starting a business was exciting to her.  She
agreed that the idea to open the store emanated with the father and a friend of
his.  She said she started to get excited and asked if she could be part of this
venture.  The father’s sister said that when the father decided not to take
this venture on, she wanted to proceed, but the father still helped her at
“every step”;

(b)

The
father claimed that he only “assisted” with financing the business.  At the
same time, he claimed to be responsible for “operations and compliance” in the
business.  He referred to himself as a “stake holder”, distinguishing this from
ownership.  So did his sister.  What they meant by that, is that he financed
the purchase of the business to the tune of $400,000.00, if not more.  Both he
and his sister would have the Court characterize this sum as a “loan” to the
father’s sister, as opposed to the money the father paid to purchase the store;

(c)

Although
both the father and his sister claimed that the father chose not to pursue the
venture and that the sister would do so without him, in cross-examination, the
father admitted that he found the business, and negotiated the purchase himself
“for the most part”, including the purchase price.  The father admitted that he
was involved in the transition of the business between owners.  He testified
that his name would have been on some of the initial purchase documents.  These
documents were not produced (or if they were, they were not tendered as exhibits);

(d)

The
father’s sister’s trial affidavit states that she returned to work in February
of 2023.  This was four months before the marijuana store “officially” opened.
She attempted to explain this away, claiming that she was able to manage a
“largely self-operational business while continuing in my full-time role” at
the insurance company.  But she also said she does not pay herself anything,
because the company is not making enough money and she was prepared to
“sacrifice”;

(e)

Not
only were the purchase documents respecting the store not tendered as exhibits
at this trial, but the corporate records concerning the marijuana business that
were introduced, were minimal.  The father tendered the Articles of
Corporation, which lists the father’s sister as the first director.  The
Articles do not specify who the shareholder(s) are;

(f)

When
earlier asked if he had produced all of the documents regarding the purchase of
the marijuana business and its operation, the father testified that his lawyer
told him to obtain certain documents to show the business was not his, but he
knew there were other documents that he did not produce.  These included
company bank statements.  He even tried to blame Ms. Yehia for any of his non-productions,
saying she did not make herself available to question his sister, prior to this
trial;

(g)

In
response to specific questions from the Court about the financing, the father
said that he took $425,000.00 from T. Investments (despite it apparently having
a $3 million liability related to a pending lawsuit).  He later said the money
came from T. Investments and TB, and from himself.  Yet when responding to the
mother’s assertion that he is still working in the financial investments
industry, the father claimed to have little to no funds, and excessive
liabilities.  And again in his trial affidavit, the father said TB was never
operational.  I was not pointed to any records that showed where the funds came
from to finance the purchase of this marijuana business, or how that withdrawal
of $400,000.00 (or more), from somewhere, was accounted for by the father;

(h)

The
father also claimed he had to take multiple loans from his mother and sister in
the past to maintain the Thornhill Property, to fund the litigation and to pay
for therapy.   Why or how the father could afford to loan money to his sister
to purchase the marijuana business, when he had to borrow from family, was not
explained;

(i)

The father’s failure to introduce documentary exhibits at this trial,
included that there was no loan agreement introduced.  No loan agreement was
introduced because there is no written loan agreement.  This alleged loan was
apparently agreed to orally between the father and his sister;

(j)

I heard conflicting accounts of what the terms of the purchase and the
loan even were between the two.  For example, when he was confronted in
cross-examination with the suggestion that his sister had not put any money towards
the purchase price, the father testified that she had paid $20,000.00 for some
of the original licenses, or maybe a bit less.  The father’s sister later
contradicted the father’s evidence that she had actually contributed something
to the start-up costs, and said that she did not put any money down.  There
were also conflicting accounts as between the two, about whether the father had
access to the business’ bank account;

(k)

I also
heard conflicting accounts of whether the father’s sister is in default of the
loan terms, whatever they allegedly may be.  I heard about this alongside the
evidence about what the father is actually paid for his work, when he started
to be paid, and what his responsibilities are;

(l)

The
father and his sister would have the Court believe that the father’s sister only
decided to bring the father “officially” onto the payroll only in March of
2024, because he was “struggling financially”.  I was told that the father is
paid “consulting” income of $48,000.00, only since that time;

(m)

The Court heard
this particular explanation from the father’s sister after first hearing from
the father himself, that he works at the business between 4 and 5 hours per
day.  While he testified that he helps with matters like compliance and there
are employees who do the “day to day” work, he also admitted that he orders
supplies, he oversees the employees, and he pays vendors.  His sister said that
he gathers the records needed for accounting, but she deals with the
accountant;

(n)

The
father attempted to explain away the amount of work that he had been doing for
the business, for free, after apparently deciding he did not want to take on
the venture in the first place, by saying that he has “obligations” for the
money he “loaned” to his sister.  He said that he needs to make sure that it
gets paid back.  The father said when his sister decided to go back to work, he
was “forced” to manage the business to ensure that he would be repaid, because
the business may not succeed without him.  He said his sister was in
“default”;  and

(o)

This
stood in contrast with the sister’s claim, above, that the business is
self-operational.  And the father’s sister then contradicted the father’s claim
that the loan was “in default”, saying that the loan was interest free, and
that is the “beauty” of doing business with family.

(5)

The
Father’s Failure to Provide All of the Disclosure Needed to Determine His
Income

[
612
]

It is the father’s onus to prove his income.  At
¶
81

of
Meade
v. Meade,
2002 CanLii 2806
(Ont. S.C.J.)
,
Kiteley J. held that
it was incumbent on those who are self-employed to put forward adequate and
comprehensive records of income and expenses, which means a package from which
the recipient spouse can draw conclusions and the amount of child support can
be established.  Where disclosure is inadequate and inferences are to be
drawn, they should be favourable to the spouse confronted with the challenge of
making sense out of the financial disclosure, and against the spouse who failed
to meet his obligation.

[
613
]

The disclosure obligations set out in
section 21
of the
Guidelines

require the parties to provide three years of tax returns and in the
mother’s case (as an employee), her most recent statement of earnings.    Because
he has been self-employed and owned corporations in the years since 2022, the father
was required to provide financial statements and statements showing a breakdown
of all salaries, wages, management fees or other payments or benefit paid to,
or on behalf of, persons or corporations with him the parent does not deal at
arm’s length.  He did not do so.

[
614
]

The
mother’s counsel attempted to embark upon questioning the father about his
non-disclosure.  Given the length of the trial I directed the parties to have
discussions about a Statement of Agreed Facts summarizing what was outstanding,
as an alternative to hearing a lengthy and likely confrontational
cross-examination about outstanding disclosure.  To their credit, they did
that.  Exhibit 113 is the parties’ Statement of Agreed Facts dated July 16,
2025.

[
615
]

While
there are some outstanding items relating to the mother, none of it was
particularly material or referred to during submissions.  In the father’s case,
there were missing tax returns and financial statements relating to T.
Investments and TB, the marijuana business’ bank statements were not supplied,
and various corporate documents, like general ledgers were not supplied.   In
my view, this is material non-disclosure when it comes to the determination of
the father’s income.

[
616
]

Nonetheless,
both the father and the mother tendered some documentation relevant to the
father’s income.  In addition, at the end of the trial, the mother introduced
voluminous bank statements of the father’s.  But neither side then asked all
the questions needed about a number of these documents, for me to analyze the
father’s income on a better or more refined basis.  Being mindful of the
principles that Kiteley J. set out in
Meade v. Meade
,
I do intend to
impute an income to the father.  However
I cannot
undertake that exercise with complete precision given the missing documents and
the manner in which questions were asked, or not asked.  Even when imputing, the
Court also still has to balance, somehow, the extent to which it will impute so
that the eventual child support order does not go too far and become
excessive.  Problems will be created if the right balance is not struck,
including the prospect of further litigation that may impact the child directly
or indirectly.

[
619
]

The

As A Litmus Test

[

]

of the

.

]

]

[
651
]

Still,
because I do not have operating expenses for subsequent years, I do not have

the simplest thing to do is work with the unaudited financial statement for the

claim that the operating expenses increased after the fiscal year ending
November 30, 2023, because for example she did renovations to the store.

[
652
]

The
next issue is whether there should be any add backs of some of the expenses
deducted.  Once again here, only some questions were posed about the other
operating expenses on the unaudited financial statement ending November 30,
2023, not comprehensive ones.  It was not just the father who did not testify
about this during his examination-in-chief, or call this evidence from his
sister;  this includes Ms. Yehia’s failure to question on a number of the
entries in cross-examination.   But returning to Kiteley J.’s analysis, it is ultimately
the father’s onus to prove his income and he should have called this evidence.
Adverse inferences can be used to add back expenses in the circumstances, at
least those which seem on their face to be unreasonable.

[
653
]

After
the operating expenses, there was net income of $27,979.00 as of the fiscal year
ending November 30, 2023. I did not otherwise hear a satisfactory explanation,
as to why those retained earnings should remain in the company.  And the
retained earnings shown of $27,979.00 are for only a half year, according to
the sister’s testimony about when the business became operational.  To
annualize them, I will multiple them by two.

[
654
]

Despite
the absence of more comprehensive questioning on some of the other expenses, I
am at a loss to understand why a marijuana store has an “automobile expense”.  Perhaps
there is a good reason for this, but this was not explained.  I would add this
back to the pre-tax corporate income under
section 18(2)
of the
Guidelines
.
To annualize this, it has to be multiplied by two also.

[
655
]

There
is also a depreciation expense, associated with furniture, computers, leasehold
improvements and signs, that was not otherwise explained.  A deduction for
depreciation may or may not be allowed when calculating income for support.  In
the absence of an explanation about this from the father, I would add this back
too:  see
Ward v. Murphy ¶ 81.
Although unhelpfully no one also told me
this, I will assume that the accountant applied a depreciation expense for the
entire year, so I will not double this expense.

[
656
]

I
do not give effect to the argument in the mother’s closing submissions, that
the professional fees deducted of $21,872.00 are necessarily personal and
should be added back, at least in 2023.  I do note that this was a newly
acquired business and perhaps there would have been higher than normal professional
fees.  In future years though, this expense may very well be less.

[
657
]

The
other obvious expense worthy of inquiry was the salary expense on the unaudited
financial statement of $79,878.00.  What I heard, in response to my question, was
that there are other employees to whom this salary expense is paid.  But that
means that the father allegedly went unpaid as he and his sister testified,
throughout 2023, and the first part of 2024.    Supplementing this particular
incredible claim, attached to his financial statement sworn October 24, 2024 is
a letter dated April 11, 2024 signed by the father’s sister, as the “Director”
of the marijuana store, purporting to confirm this.  The letter says that the
father is engaged in a “consulting contract” with the marijuana business.  The
letter says that the “contract terms” are as follows:

-

Consulting services for compliances and operations of [the business]

-

Payment of $4,000.00 per month

-

6 month term for the period of February 2024 to July 2024

-

The contract may be renewed at the discretion of [the business]

[
658
]

A
duplicate of this letter, and another one dated May 13, 2025, containing the
same terms, except now for a 12-month period between July 2024 and July 2025,
were entered as separate exhibits.

[
659
]

As
I do not have any other data to figure out a reasonable salary for his work, at
a minimum, I find it appropriate to use the father’s and his sister’s own
letter as an admission, to impute that level of income to him.  As he did not report
income to the Canada Revenue Agency in the past, I will gross this amount up, using
DivorceMate.  While I don’t believe that he worked for free in 2023, even if he
did, that was not a reasonable thing to do.

[
660
]

Therefore,
my calculation of the money available to be drawn from the marijuana business,
combined with the father’s grossed up salary or consulting fees, is set out in
the Chart below.  A DivorceMate calculation is also attached as
Schedule “A”

to show the gross up
.
It adds up to just over $184,000.00.  This litmus
test is close enough to the $200,000.00 being imputed to him.  If I am correct
and the professional fees reduce in subsequent years, then my calculation would
be higher, perhaps at the $200,000.00 level.  As would the calculation if I
should have grossed up the add back at the corporate level, for the automobile
expense.

(13)

Both Parties’ Rental Income

[
661
]

Both
parties have earned rental income at times.  I have not made an adjustment to
either party’s incomes for this.  Neither party reported any of the rental
income earned to the Canada Revenue Agency, so I had no Statement of Rentals in
either of their tax returns.

[
662
]

Neither
side provided me with any calculations of what adjustments to both parties
income should be made for this anyway.  For example, I was not told what
expenses should be deducted from the gross rental income earned, to determine
what net rental income to attribute to the parties.  I was not given a gross up
calculation for this either, given that any net rental income earned was not
reported.

[
663
]

In
the mother’s case regarding the Thornhill Property in particular, I am not
ordering a post-separation accounting of the rental income for the reasons
expressed elsewhere, as such I would not make any adjustments to her income for
this.  Regarding rental income earned at her rental, the mother testified that
she is no longer earning rental income there.  The father testified there is no
tenant in the basement of the Thornhill Property anymore, since March of 2025.
So perhaps nothing would be added for this year anyway.

[
664
]

Had
I added some adjusted rental income from the Thornhill Property to the income
available from the marijuana business for prior years though, like 2023 when
rental income was earned, I note that this too would have put the father even
closer to the $200,000.00 being imputed to him, than the $184,000.00 number
calculated in the chart above.

[
665
]

In
the future if rental income continues to be earned by one or the other party,
this will have to be disclosed and may be considered in a future review or
variation of child support.  But a proper analysis of the net rental income needs
to be done by the parties.

(14)

Conclusions Respecting the Father’s Income

[
666
]

In
the result, I have decided to impute an income of
$200,000.00
to the
father in all years since the Separation Agreement.  Although imprecise, I find
it likely approximates what the situation was when the parties entered into the
Separation Agreement, and what was available to the father (from the marijuana
business or otherwise), starting in the next year, which was 2023.  It is a
sufficient level of income to meet the original annual budget on father’s
family law financial statement, before he reduced his sworn budget for some
reason unexplained.

F.   Findings and Conclusions Regarding the Mother’s Claim for
Retroactive Child Support Between the April 1, 2022 and the Beginning of 2025,
and Child Support Commencing February 1, 2025

[
667
]

Therefore,
while I agree that the father’s income was higher than the mother’s in the
past, when I impute an income of $200,000.00 to the father, the $500.00 monthly
amount of child support in the Separation Agreement is more or less a set off.
In the absence of submissions about a proper
section 9
analysis for the period
between 2022 and January of 2025, I would not change the amount of support in
the Separation Agreement, until early 2025.  I am not in a position to find
that the amount to which the parties agreed, departs from what the
Guidelines

would have provided, without those further submissions.  And because of all
this, I do not find, having regard to
section 56(1.1)
of the
Family Law Act
,

that what they agreed to in the Separation Agreement was not reasonable, at
least until the beginning of 2025 when the parenting schedule changed.

[
668
]

However
I find that the monthly support provision in the Separation Agreement should be
disregarded after January 28, 2025, not based on changes in income, but because
the child began residing with the mother primarily.  $500.00 per month is no
longer reasonable as of that time.

[
669
]

Therefore,
I find the father shall pay child support to the mother in the amount of $1,659.00
commencing February 1, 2025.  This is the table amount of child support for one
child, based on imputed income of $200,000.00 per annum.  As indicated earlier,
the new table amount of child support as of October 1, 2025 is $1,707.00.  The
father is entitled to a credit of $500.00 for February 2025.  The father
stopped paying child support after that, and so there are no further credits to
apply.

G.

Section
7 Expenses

[
670
]

The
parties agreed to share section 7 expenses equally in the Separation
Agreement.  I did not hear any complaint that there were section 7 expenses
prior to 2025 that were not shared.  With the exception of some section 7
expenses incurred so far this year, a claim for retroactive section 7 expenses prior
to 2025 was not pursued during this trial.

[
671
]

The
situation is different going forward.  The mother’s draft Order proposes an
uneven proportionate sharing based on the discrepancy in the parties’ incomes.
While I do not adopt her proposed percentages (as they are based on her
different income determination for the father), based on the Court’s imputation
at $200,000.00, for 2025 going forward, the percentage sharing is 60% (father),
40% (mother).

[
672
]

Paragraph
29 of the mother’s draft Order sets out a list of section 7 expenses that the
mother testified she incurs for the child.  While I did hear some evidence from
her about how much various items cost and what she paid, she did not set out a
monthly amount for the father’s contribution.  Therefore I will only order the
father to pay 60% of the expenses in the list commencing February 1, 2025,
without quantifying them.

[
673
]

However
I am prepared to quantify a retroactive award for section 7 expenses already
paid from February 1, 2025 until now if the mother wants, because I heard some evidence
about what she has already paid for in the first part of 2025, and that the
father did not contribute.  I am not prepared to figure this out on my own.  I
am directing the parties to quantify the amount of section 7 expenses owing to
the mother from February 1, 2025 until now, by applying paragraph 29 of the
mother’s draft Order and the percentage sharing set out above, to the evidence
tendered at this trial.  If the parties cannot agree, then each side may
provide me with a brief chart containing the calculations when the file their
costs submissions, and I will entertain quantifying an amount owing between February
1, 2025 and now.

[
674
]

The
parties are cautioned to make every effort to sort this out first, and not to
turn this simple accounting issue into another round of hotly contested
litigation.  If they do, this too may be relevant when it comes to costs.

H.

Future
Motions to Change Child Support

[
675
]

The
Court’s Order below includes very specific disclosure requirements for future
years.  The mother can move for an upward variation in the future if she
wishes, based on fuller disclosure once she gets it, and a fuller income
analysis.

[
676
]

Incredibly,
during closing submissions, the father’s counsel told the Court, that if the
Court found the father was the true owner of the marijuana business and imputed
an income to him on that basis, that “might necessitate [the father] bringing a
Motion to Change”.

[
677
]

I
invite the father, to review with his counsel, the requirement to obtain leave during
the six months that follow a support Order, that is set out in
section 37(3)
of
the
Family Law Act
.
I also invite the father and his counsel to review
Pazaratz J.’s decision in in
Trang v. Trang,
2013 ONSC 1980
,
respecting
the legal test that applies to vary child support, when income has been imputed
.

Even after the passage of six months, the father is not just at liberty to
bring a Motion to Change, and simply rely on his Line 150 Income, which so far
is basically 0, just because he may be dissatisfied with the outcome in this
Judgment.

[
678
]

In
view of the father’s cavalier attitude about his disclosure and child support
obligations, I intend to make an order requiring the father to obtain leave
before bringing a Motion to Change child support, including after the six
months set out in
section 37(3)
of the
Family Law Act
.  I will set out
what will be required for him to obtain leave.  There needs to be some judicial
oversight over the provision of disclosure to prevent a repeat of what happened
here.  In so doing, I am also mindful again (just as I was careful in
exercising restraint in the imputing exercise not create a too high Order, not
supported by the evidence, that will just spur more litigation), that it is in
this child’s best interests for this litigation (and for future litigation
where possible) to stop.

I.

Life Insurance and Health Benefits

679
]

The
mother’s draft Order includes terms that the father shall maintain life

¶
